notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Cache-aside** — App checks cache, falls back to DB, populates cache — flexible, with the stale-read risk you must name.
- **Read-through / write-through** — Read-through: the cache loads from the DB itself. Write-through: writes go to cache and DB together — consistent, slower writes.
- **TTL and invalidation** — Time-to-live bounds staleness; the invalidation strategy is caching's permanent tax — every caching decision must name it.
- **Thundering herd** — A hot key expires and every request stampedes the DB — stopped by request coalescing (single-flight), probabilistic early refresh, or staggered TTLs with jitter.
- **Redis data structures** — Strings (counters, rate limits), hashes (objects), lists (queues), sets (membership), sorted sets (leaderboards, time-ordered feeds) — five tools, one store.
- **At-least-once delivery** — The practical default: retries can duplicate — made safe by idempotent consumers, which is effectively exactly-once processing.
- **Exactly-once semantics** — Needs idempotent consumers or transactions (Kafka EOS) — the honest answer names the machinery, not the wish.
- **Kafka** — Distributed commit log: topics split into partitions (the parallelism unit), consumer groups split partitions across consumers, offsets track progress — ordering guaranteed per partition only.
- **Backpressure** — Bounded queues that block or shed so the producer feels the consumer's slowness — an unbounded queue is a deferred outage.
- **Dead-letter queue** — Where poison messages go after retries exhaust: quarantine for inspection instead of blocking the stream or looping forever.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Implement cache-aside for one read path in a toy app: read, miss, load, populate — then write the invalidation rule for the corresponding write path.
2. Simulate a thundering herd: expire a hot key under synthetic load, observe the DB spike, then add single-flight coalescing and re-run — compare the curves.
3. Model three features in Redis data structures (a leaderboard, a rate limiter, a job queue): pick the structure per feature and state why the others don't fit.
4. Design a consumer for at-least-once delivery: write the idempotency check (processed-IDs set), the retry policy, and the dead-letter routing for poison messages.
5. Sketch a Kafka topic for an order pipeline: choose the partition key, state the ordering guarantee it gives, and assign consumer groups for two independent consumers.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Cache-and-queue architecture brief. For the order pipeline: the caching layer (what is cached, the strategy per path, TTLs, the invalidation plan, the herd defense), and the queue topology (topics/queues, partition keys, consumer groups, retry and dead-letter policy, the backpressure story). Include the failure modes: cache outage, consumer lag, poison message. Deliverable: the brief — the section that proves you design for the unhappy path.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: caching and queue topologies are capacity-shaped — the right answers change with traffic, budget, and the managed services you actually run, and this course confers no certificate. The interview rewards naming failure modes honestly; production rewards measuring them.

**Problem.** A bounded queue with a drop-or-block policy implements:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Backpressure — the producer feels the consumer’s slowness
- **Why:** Bounded buffers propagate slowness upstream instead of growing memory until collapse.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Bounded buffers propagate slowness upstream instead of growing memory until collapse.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In Caching and Message Queues, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in Caching and Message Queues gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

modules.summary: Welcome to Caching and Message Queues — module 3 of the Backend path. I'm your instructor, and this is scale's two workhorses: caches that absorb reads and queues that absorb bursts — with the failure modes (stampedes, poison messages) interviewers love to ask about. We cover cache-aside/read-through/write-through, TTL and invalidation, Redis data structures in practice, delivery semantics, Kafka topics/partitions/consumer groups, and backpressure with dead-letter queues. By the end, you will pair every speedup with its invalidation story.

cards.front: Threads vs processes vs event loops?
cards.back: Processes: isolated memory, expensive. Threads: shared memory, cheap-ish, need locks. Event loop: single-threaded async I/O (Node, asyncio) — great for I/O-bound, terrible for CPU-bound. Match the model to the bottleneck.

cards.front: How do you explain deadlock prevention?
cards.back: Deadlock needs four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) — break any one: lock ordering (always acquire in the same global order) is the classic fix. In an interview, draw the wait cycle, then name the broken condition.

cards.front: What is backpressure, and where do you put it?
cards.back: When consumers are slower than producers, pressure must go somewhere: bounded queues that block/shed, reactive streams with demand signaling, or Kafka consumer-lag alerting. The interview point: an unbounded queue is a deferred outage.

cards.front: Token bucket vs leaky bucket — which allows bursts?
cards.back: Token bucket: tokens accumulate up to capacity, so short bursts above the sustained rate are allowed. Leaky bucket: requests queue and drain at a constant rate — smooth output, no bursts. State which behavior the product needs.

cards.front: Why is distributed locking hard, and what’s the Redis answer?
cards.back: Locks must survive holder crashes (TTL/lease) and clock issues; naive SETNX without expiry deadlocks on crash. The pattern: SET with NX + PX expiry, fencing tokens for ordering, and always keep the critical section short.

cards.front: How do you explain the C10K problem’s modern answer?
cards.back: Blocking thread-per-connection dies near ten thousand concurrent connections; the answers are event loops and now virtual threads or goroutines — cheap concurrency units with blocking-style code. The interview line: ‘the fix was never faster threads; it was cheaper ones.’

cards.front: What is lock ordering, and when do you name it?
cards.back: Acquire multiple locks in a globally consistent order to break the circular-wait condition — the practical deadlock fix. Name it whenever the design takes two locks. The interview line: ‘ordered locks make deadlock structurally impossible.’

cards.front: How do you size a rate limiter’s storage?
cards.back: Counters per key per window: memory equals keys times window entries — Redis with TTL expiry bounds it naturally. Sliding-window logs are precise but heavy; fixed windows are cheap but edge-bursty. The interview line: ‘the limiter’s memory is the price of its precision.’

cards.front: An idempotent pipeline stage guarantees:
cards.back: **Reprocessing the same input produces the same output — no duplicates** — Reruns are inevitable; idempotency makes them safe.

cards.front: A distributed lock MUST have an expiry because:
cards.back: **A crashed holder would otherwise hold the lock forever** — Without TTL, a holder that dies mid-section deadlocks every waiter — the lease bounds the damage.

cards.front: An API that should allow brief traffic spikes should use:
cards.back: **Token bucket** — Accumulated tokens absorb bursts up to bucket capacity; a leaky bucket would queue or drop them.

cards.front: A bounded queue with a drop-or-block policy implements:
cards.back: **Backpressure — the producer feels the consumer’s slowness** — Bounded buffers propagate slowness upstream instead of growing memory until collapse.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Threads vs processes vs event loops** — Processes: isolated, expensive. Threads: shared memory, need locks. Event loops: single-threaded async I/O — great for I/O-bound, terrible for CPU-bound.
- **Deadlock's four conditions** — Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — break any one; lock ordering (global acquisition order) is the classic fix.
- **Backpressure** — When consumers lag producers, pressure must go somewhere: bounded queues, demand signaling, consumer-lag alerting — never an unbounded queue.
- **Token bucket** — Tokens accumulate to capacity: sustained rate plus short bursts allowed — the limiter for APIs that should tolerate spikes.
- **Leaky bucket** — Requests queue and drain at a constant rate: smooth output, no bursts — the limiter for steady downstream capacity.
- **Distributed lock (Redis)** — SET with NX + PX expiry, fencing tokens for ordering, short critical sections — because a crashed holder without a TTL deadlocks every waiter.
- **Idempotent consumers** — Reprocessing the same input yields the same output — the concurrency-safe way to survive duplicate deliveries and retries.
- **Race condition** — Outcome depends on uncontrolled scheduling interleaving — fixed by making the critical section atomic or the operation idempotent.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write a tiny multithreaded counter with and without a lock; run it under contention and observe the lost updates — then fix it and state which hazard you removed.
2. Draw a deadlock from two locks acquired in opposite orders; then impose a global lock ordering and show the cycle can't form — state the broken condition aloud.
3. Implement a token bucket and a leaky bucket for the same API: configure burst tolerance on one and smooth output on the other, and state which product need each serves.
4. Build the Redis distributed-lock pattern (SET NX PX + fencing token + short critical section); then kill the holder mid-section and verify the TTL bounds the damage.
5. Design the backpressure story for one pipeline: bounded queue depth, the drop-or-block policy, the alert on consumer lag — and the load-shedding rule when it fills.

cards.front: How do you decompose a monolith in a design interview?
cards.back: By bounded contexts (DDD): split along business capabilities with clean ownership, not technical layers. Each service owns its data; cross-service needs go through APIs or events. And name the honest counterargument: start modular-monolith until the seams are proven.

cards.front: Sync vs async service communication?
cards.back: Sync (REST/gRPC): simple, but couples availability and latency — a slow downstream slows you. Async (queues/events): decoupled, resilient, but eventual consistency and harder debugging. The interview line: ‘sync for queries needing answers now, async for work that can wait.’

cards.front: What do service discovery and API gateways do?
cards.back: Service discovery: services find each other’s current addresses as instances churn (registry or DNS-based). API gateway: single entry point handling routing, auth, rate limiting, and aggregation for clients.

cards.front: Distributed transactions: what’s the saga answer?
cards.back: No 2PC across services — use sagas: a sequence of local transactions where each step has a compensating action (refund, cancel) for rollback. Choreography (events) for simple flows, orchestration (a saga coordinator) when the flow needs central control.

cards.front: Logs, metrics, traces — when do you reach for each?
cards.back: Metrics: ‘is something wrong’ (alerts, dashboards). Logs: ‘what happened’ (discrete events with context). Traces: ‘where did the request go’ (latency across services). The interview line: ‘metrics alert me, traces show me where, logs tell me why.’

cards.front: How do you discuss the strangler-fig migration?
cards.back: Wrap the monolith, route new capabilities to new services behind the facade, carve off bounded contexts one at a time — the monolith shrinks until it can be retired. The interview line: ‘strangler-fig is the only rewrite strategy that ships every week.’

cards.front: What breaks first in a microservices design answer?
cards.back: The network: latency budgets across hops, cascading failures, and version skew between services. Answers: timeouts with budgets, bulkheads, backward-compatible contracts. The interview line: ‘distributed systems fail at the seams — design the seams.’

cards.front: How do you talk about service meshes honestly?
cards.back: mTLS, retries, and observability without code changes — at the cost of a sidecar per pod (latency, memory, operational complexity). Worth it at dozens of services; overhead below that. The interview line: ‘the mesh buys uniformity; check the price in tail latency.’

cards.front: A modular monolith is often the right starting point because:
cards.back: **It keeps bounded-context discipline without paying the distributed-systems tax prematurely** — Distribution is a cost; pay it when a proven seam demands independent scaling or ownership.

cards.front: A distributed trace’s primary value is:
cards.back: **Following one request across services to find where latency/errors originate** — Trace spans stitch the request path across service boundaries — the only view that crosses them.

cards.front: A saga handles failure of step 3 in a 5-step flow by:
cards.back: **Running compensating actions for steps 1–2** — Each completed step’s compensating transaction semantically undoes it — the distributed answer to rollback.

cards.front: An API gateway centralizes:
cards.back: **Cross-cutting edge concerns: routing, auth, rate limiting for inbound traffic** — One policy-enforcement point at the edge beats reimplementing auth and limits in every service.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Bounded contexts** — DDD decomposition along business capabilities with clean ownership — split by capability, not by technical layer; each service owns its data.
- **Sync vs async** — Sync (REST/gRPC): simple, couples availability and latency. Async (queues/events): decoupled and resilient, but eventually consistent and harder to debug.
- **Service discovery** — How services find each other's current addresses as instances churn — registry or DNS-based; the answer to 'what's the URL?' in a dynamic fleet.
- **API gateway** — Single entry point: routing, auth, rate limiting, aggregation for clients — cross-cutting edge concerns in one policy point.
- **Saga** — Distributed transactions without 2PC: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action — choreography (events) for simple flows, orchestration (coordinator) for complex ones.
- **Observability trio** — Metrics: 'is something wrong' (alerts). Logs: 'what happened' (events with context). Traces: 'where did the request go' (latency across services).
- **Modular monolith** — Bounded-context discipline inside one deployable — the honest starting point until a proven seam demands distribution.
- **Distributed-systems tax** — The permanent costs of distribution: network failures, eventual consistency, observability burden, deployment complexity — paid only for proven seams.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Decompose a familiar monolith (an e-commerce app) into bounded contexts on paper: name the contexts, draw the ownership lines, and state what data each service owns.
2. For each cross-service call in your decomposition, choose sync or async and write the one-sentence justification ('sync: the user waits for this answer; async: this work can wait').
3. Design the saga for an order flow (payment → inventory → notification): list the steps, write each compensating action, and choose choreography vs orchestration with reasons.
4. Write the observability plan: which metrics alert, what the logs carry per request (correlation IDs), and where traces would have found the last incident you remember.
5. Argue the counter-case: write the modular-monolith version of your decomposition and name the exact conditions (scale seam, team seam) that would flip you to services.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Decomposition brief. Take the order pipeline and write the microservices decision document: bounded contexts with ownership, the sync/async map, the saga with compensating actions, service discovery and gateway placement, and the observability plan (metrics, logs, traces with correlation). Close with the honest counterargument: the modular-monolith alternative and the conditions that would change the call. Deliverable: the brief — distribution argued, not assumed.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: microservices advice is org-shaped — team size, deployment maturity, and domain complexity change the answer, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers reward the tradeoff argument; the industry's hype cycles are not engineering evidence.

notes.title: Worked example: A modular monolith is often the right starting point because:
notes.body:
**Problem.** A modular monolith is often the right starting point because:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** It keeps bounded-context discipline without paying the distributed-systems tax prematurely
- **Why:** Distribution is a cost; pay it when a proven seam demands independent scaling or ownership.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Distribution is a cost; pay it when a proven seam demands independent scaling or ownership.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In Microservices Architecture, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in Microservices Architecture gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

cards.front: How do you design a rate-limited public API?
cards.back: Requirements (limits per key/IP, burst policy) → token-bucket in Redis with atomic Lua → 429 + RateLimit-* headers + Retry-After → per-endpoint tiers. The interview line: ‘the limiter is part of the API contract, not an afterthought.’

cards.front: How do you design an order pipeline with queues?
cards.back: API accepts and validates → order events to a queue → workers for payment, inventory, notification (each with retries + DLQ) → saga/compensation for failures. The interview line: ‘the queue is the seam where reliability lives.’

cards.front: What goes in an API contract / OpenAPI sketch?
cards.back: Endpoints, methods, request/response schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits, and versioning — enough that a client team could build against it. The interview line: ‘the contract is the interface; code is the implementation.’

cards.front: k6 vs JMeter — how do you compare them?
cards.back: k6: JS-scripted, developer-friendly, great for CI-integrated load tests with thresholds as gates. JMeter: GUI-driven, mature, huge protocol support, heavier. The interview line: ‘k6 for code-reviewed load tests in the pipeline; JMeter where the team already lives in it.’

cards.front: What goes in a failure-mode writeup?
cards.back: For each component: how it fails, blast radius, detection (which alert fires), mitigation (what the responder does), and whether degradation is graceful. The interview line: ‘I design the unhappy path with the same care as the happy one.’

cards.front: How do you design a URL shortener’s write path?
cards.back: Accept the URL → validate and normalize → generate the ID (counter + base62 or a key-generation service) → check custom-alias uniqueness → persist the mapping → warm the cache. The interview line: ‘the write path is where collisions and duplicates get decided.’

cards.front: What goes in a load-test plan for the build?
cards.back: The forecast peak at 1.5×, a soak run for leaks, a spike run for autoscaling lag — with pass/fail thresholds as CI gates. The interview line: ‘a load test without a gate is just a graph.’

cards.front: How do you present the build’s architecture in an interview?
cards.back: One diagram, three layers: the request path, the data path, and the failure paths — then the two hardest decisions with rejected alternatives. The interview line: ‘the diagram shows what; the decisions show judgment.’

cards.front: Ending a design round with open tradeoffs is strong because:
cards.back: **It shows judgment about what matters and invites collaborative discussion** — Naming what you’d revisit proves you see the design’s limits — a senior signal.

cards.front: A failure-mode writeup’s audience is:
cards.back: **The future on-call responder — it’s a pre-written triage guide** — Written calmly now, it guides panicked decisions at 3am.

cards.front: k6’s thresholds turn a load test into:
cards.back: **A gate: breaching p95/error-rate assertions fails the run** — Thresholds are pass/fail assertions on metrics — the test proves the SLO or it fails.

cards.front: Writing the contract before the implementation is strong because:
cards.back: **It forces interface decisions early, when they’re cheap — and enables parallel client/server work** — Contract-first surfaces disagreements before code cements them.

- **45-minute presentation** — The design-round cadence: requirements, estimation, API/data, deep-dive, tradeoffs — ending with the tradeoffs you'd revisit.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Estimation is order-of-magnitude judgment with stated assumptions, narrated aloud. Work each estimation below on paper, stating every assumption before the arithmetic.

1. Estimate the rate-limited API: 10k req/s sustained, 2× burst — size the Redis token-bucket state, compute per-key memory, and state the Lua atomicity requirement.
2. Estimate the order pipeline: 50k orders/day, peak 10× — queue depth for the peak hour, worker count from per-worker throughput, DLQ sizing for a 1% poison rate.
3. Write the k6 script plan for the API: stages (ramp, sustain, spike), thresholds (p95, error rate), and the gate assertion that fails the run.
4. Recompute the pipeline estimate with one changed assumption (orders 5×, or a new channel added) and name which design decision flips.
5. Present one design in 45 minutes on camera: timebox visibly, end with three tradeoffs you'd revisit — then score yourself against the rubric.

cards.back: Budget: 5 min requirements, 10 min resources + verbs + status codes, 10 min edge cases (pagination, idempotency, versioning), 5 min tradeoffs. Think in resources and contracts — the interview line: ‘I design the contract a client could program against.’

cards.front: How do you survive concurrency + data-layer deep dives?
cards.back: Name the hazards (races, deadlocks, N+1, isolation anomalies), then the tools (locks with ordering, idempotent consumers, eager loading, right isolation level) — each tied to a concrete scenario. The interview line: ‘I answer hazards with mechanisms, not buzzwords.’

cards.front: What’s a behavioral ledger?
cards.back: Your running record: story bank entries, which stories you’ve told where, feedback received, and follow-up questions that stumped you. It stops you from repeating the same story and turns each behavioral round into training data.

cards.front: What makes a mock interview actually improve you?
cards.back: The debrief loop: within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), pick the single biggest leak, and redrill it within 48 hours. Mocks without debriefs are just stage fright practice.

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

cards.front: How do you handle the ‘design it, then scale it 10x’ follow-up?
cards.back: Find the first bottleneck on the request path, apply the standard lever (cache, shard, queue), re-estimate, repeat. The interview line: ‘scaling is bottleneck whack-a-mole with math.’

cards.front: What do you do when the interviewer goes silent?

cards.front: Explain closures like the interviewer is testing depth.
cards.back: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope — the variables live as long as the closure does. That’s the module pattern, private state, and also the classic bug: loop variables captured by reference (fixed with let in modern JS).

cards.front: How do you explain ‘this’ and prototypes without rambling?
cards.back: ‘this’ is set by the call site (method call, plain call, new, arrow functions inherit lexically). Prototypes are the delegation chain: property lookup walks up the chain. Classes are syntax over the same prototype mechanism.

cards.front: Microtasks vs macrotasks — the interview-ready version?
cards.back: The event loop drains the microtask queue (promises, queueMicrotask) completely after each macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, rendering steps). So promise callbacks run before setTimeout(0) — and a microtask loop can starve rendering.

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in promises/async-await?
cards.back: Error paths: unhandled rejections, try/catch around await, Promise.all failing fast vs allSettled for independent work, and never mixing raw callbacks with await. The senior signal: ‘here’s how this fails and how the caller learns about it.’

cards.front: What TypeScript features do interviewers actually ask about?
cards.back: Narrowing (typeof/instanceof/discriminated unions — exhaustiveness checking with never), generics with constraints, and utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record). The pitch: ‘types as executable documentation that the compiler checks.’

cards.front: How do you explain the event loop’s interview edge cases?
cards.back: queueMicrotask vs promise ordering, setTimeout(0) still waiting for the current task, and starving the loop with microtask recursion. The interview line: ‘microtasks drain completely — that is the whole trick.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in TypeScript narrowing?
cards.back: typeof and instanceof guards, discriminated unions, and exhaustiveness checking with never — the compiler proving you handled every case. The interview line: ‘narrowing is the compiler finishing your if-statements.’

cards.front: How do you discuss memory leaks in frontend interviews?
cards.back: Detached DOM nodes held by closures, forgotten event listeners and intervals, and ever-growing caches without eviction. The interview line: ‘leaks are references you forgot you kept.’

cards.front: Rehearsing the perennial questions pays off because:
cards.back: **They’re guaranteed points — fluency here buys composure for the novel problems** — Banking the predictable questions preserves mental budget for the unpredictable ones.

cards.front: A discriminated union’s power in TypeScript is:
cards.back: **Exhaustive narrowing: the compiler proves you handled every variant** — Switching on the discriminant literal lets TS narrow each branch — and ‘never’ in default proves exhaustiveness.

cards.front: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled: the difference is:
cards.back: **all rejects on the first rejection; allSettled waits for every outcome** — all short-circuits on first failure; allSettled reports each promise’s fulfilled/rejected status.

cards.front: Promise.then callbacks run before setTimeout(0) callbacks because:
cards.back: **Microtasks drain fully between macrotasks** — The spec processes the entire microtask queue after each macrotask — promises always win the race.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Closure** — A function capturing its enclosing scope's variables — the variables live as long as the closure does; the module pattern, private state, and the classic captured-loop-variable bug.
- **Scope** — Where bindings are visible: function, block (let/const), and module scope — the map you read before reasoning about any variable.
- **this** — Set by the call site — method call, plain call, new, or arrow functions inheriting lexically; prototypes are the delegation chain classes sit on top of.
- **Event loop** — The runtime's scheduling loop: run a macrotask, drain the microtask queue fully, render — the model behind every async interview question.
- **Microtasks vs macrotasks** — Microtasks (promises, queueMicrotask) drain completely after each macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, rendering) — so promise callbacks run before setTimeout(0), and a microtask loop can starve rendering.
- **Promise error paths** — Unhandled rejections, try/catch around await, Promise.all failing fast versus allSettled for independent work — the senior signal is 'here's how this fails and how the caller learns about it.'
- **Narrowing** — typeof/instanceof checks and discriminated unions that shrink a type — with exhaustiveness checking via never proving every variant is handled.
- **Generics with constraints** — Type parameters bounded by constraints — reusable functions and components that stay type-safe across shapes.
- **Utility types** — Partial, Pick, Omit, Record — the standard transformations for deriving types instead of rewriting them.
- **Module pattern** — Closures used to expose a public API over private state — the pre-class encapsulation idiom that still explains how privacy works.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write the closure bug and its fix from memory: the loop-variable capture, then the let-scoped version — explain both aloud in under a minute.
2. Trace an event-loop ordering exercise by hand: interleaved promises, setTimeout(0), and queueMicrotask — predict the order, then run it to verify.
3. Convert a callback-based function to async/await with proper error paths: try/catch, an allSettled for independent calls, and no unhandled rejections.
4. Write a discriminated union with exhaustive narrowing: switch on the discriminant, put never in the default, and let the compiler prove completeness.
5. Drill the ten perennial questions aloud — two minutes each, layered: the 30-second answer, the mechanism, the classic bug — until none of them cost you composure.

cards.front: What does ‘components as functions of state’ mean?
cards.back: UI = f(state): given the same state, the component renders the same output — no hidden dependencies. It’s why unidirectional data flow works and why testing components is easy: set state, assert output. The interview line: ‘pure rendering functions; side effects at the edges.’

cards.front: Stale closures in React hooks — how do you explain the bug and the fix?
cards.back: A useEffect or useCallback closure captures state from the render when it was created — so it reads stale values on later runs. The interview line: ‘the closure sees the render it closed over, not the latest state.’ Fixes: include dependencies honestly, use functional setState updates, or read latest values through a ref without re-subscribing.

cards.front: Why do keys matter in React lists?
cards.back: Reconciliation matches old and new elements by key: stable keys let React move/reuse DOM nodes; index keys on reorderable lists cause wrong state reuse and wasted re-renders. Keys are identity, not decoration.

cards.front: memo, useMemo, useCallback — when is each the right call?
cards.back: memo: skip re-rendering a component when props are shallow-equal (for expensive subtrees). useMemo: cache an expensive computation. useCallback: stabilize a function identity passed to memoized children. And the caveat: don’t memoize everything — measure first.

cards.front: How do you discuss state management tradeoffs?
cards.back: Lift state to the lowest common parent first; context for truly global low-churn data (theme, auth) — not as a state manager, since context re-renders all consumers; external stores (Zustand/Redux) for complex shared state with selective subscriptions.

cards.front: How do you explain reconciliation in an interview?
cards.back: React diffs the new element tree against the old: same type → update props; different type → unmount and remount; lists matched by key. The interview line: ‘reconciliation is diffing with a budget — keys are how you spend it wisely.’

cards.front: When do effects cause infinite loops?
cards.back: When the effect writes state it depends on without a guard — setState inside an effect with a missing or unstable dependency array. The interview line: ‘the loop is the effect arguing with its own dependencies.’

cards.front: How do you discuss server components honestly?
cards.back: They render on the server and ship HTML plus minimal JS: smaller bundles and direct data access — but no interactivity, no browser APIs, and a split mental model. The interview line: ‘server components trade client JS for a server round-trip.’

cards.front: React Server Components primarily reduce:
cards.back: **Client-side JavaScript shipped for non-interactive UI** — Server-rendered components never hydrate: their code stays off the client bundle.

cards.front: React context is a poor state manager for high-churn state because:
cards.back: **Every consumer re-renders on any context value change** — Context has no selectors: one value change re-renders all consumers regardless of what they use.

cards.front: useCallback’s purpose is:
cards.back: **Preserving function identity across renders so memoized children don’t re-render** — A new function identity each render defeats memo on children; useCallback stabilizes it.

cards.front: Using array index as key breaks when:
cards.back: **Items reorder or are inserted — React reuses the wrong component state** — Identity must follow the item, not its position; index keys lie about identity on reorder.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **UI = f(state)** — Components as pure rendering functions of state: same state, same output — why unidirectional data flow works and why components are easy to test.
- **Hook closures** — Effects and callbacks capture the render's values — stale state is a closure problem; the fix is reading the capture, not fighting the linter.
- **Reconciliation** — React's diff of old and new trees, matched by key — stable keys let it move and reuse DOM nodes; index keys on reorderable lists cause wrong state reuse.
- **Keys as identity** — Keys are identity, not decoration: identity must follow the item, not its position.
- **memo** — Skips re-rendering a component when props are shallow-equal — for expensive subtrees, measured first, not everywhere.
- **useMemo / useCallback** — useMemo caches an expensive computation; useCallback stabilizes a function identity so memoized children don't re-render — memoize by measurement.
- **State management ladder** — Lift state to the lowest common parent → context for truly global low-churn data → external stores for complex shared state with selective subscriptions.
- **Context's re-render cost** — No selectors: one context value change re-renders all consumers — why context is a poor state manager for high-churn state.
- **Server components** — Components that render on the server and never hydrate — non-interactive UI ships less client JavaScript.
- **Render discipline** — The habit of asking 'what re-rendered and why' before optimizing — profile, then memoize the measured hotspot.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:

1. Build a tiny app with a stale-closure bug in an effect; diagnose it by naming the captured render's values, then fix it — explain the mechanism aloud.
2. Render a reorderable list with index keys, observe the wrong-state-reuse bug, switch to stable keys, and state the reconciliation rule that changed the behavior.
3. Profile a slow subtree, add memo/useMemo/useCallback at the measured hotspot only, and re-profile — write the before/after numbers.
4. Move shared state through the ladder for one feature: lifted state, then context, then an external store — state at each step what broke or got awkward.
5. Answer 'why did this re-render?' for three scenarios (parent re-render, context change, new function identity) — mechanism first, fix second.

cards.front: Reflow vs repaint vs compositing?

cards.front: LCP, INP, CLS — what does each measure?
cards.back: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): loading — when the main content appears. INP (Interaction to Next Paint): responsiveness — worst-case input latency. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): visual stability — unexpected movement. For all three, lower is better.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Critical rendering path** — Parse HTML → DOM, parse CSS → CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite — sync scripts and render-blocking CSS delay first paint.
- **Reflow** — Layout: geometry changes — expensive, cascades to descendants; the cost to avoid in animations.
- **Repaint** — Visual changes without geometry — cheaper than reflow, still per-frame budget to watch.
- **Compositing** — GPU layer moves (transform/opacity) — the cheapest visual change; the animation discipline is 'transform and opacity only.'
- **LCP** — Largest Contentful Paint: loading — when the main content appears; lower is better.
- **INP** — Interaction to Next Paint: responsiveness — worst-case input latency; lower is better.
- **CLS** — Cumulative Layout Shift: visual stability — unexpected movement; lower is better.
- **Flame-chart reading** — Record an interaction, read the long tasks, layout/paint blocks, and JS stacks — the bottleneck decides the fix, not intuition.
- **Code splitting** — Ship only what the route needs: route-level splits plus lazy loading cut initial JS — and parse/compile time is the real mobile bottleneck.
- **Resource hints** — preload (high-priority, current page) vs prefetch (low-priority, likely next navigation) — intent and priority, declared up front.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Open DevTools Performance on a slow page you know: record an interaction, identify the longest task, and name the category (scripting, rendering, network) before proposing any fix.
2. Fix one layout-thrash pattern: batch DOM reads and writes, or move an animation to transform/opacity — re-measure and write the before/after.
3. Audit a page's vitals: find LCP, INP, CLS, name the likely cause of the worst one, and propose the single highest-leverage fix.
4. Add route-level code splitting to a toy app: measure initial JS before and after with the coverage panel — state the parse/compile saving.
5. Write the perf-investigation script you'd narrate in an interview: profile → bottleneck → fix → re-measure — and rehearse it on one real page.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Performance case study. Take a slow page (a demo app or a public page you can analyze): profile it, identify the bottleneck with flame-chart evidence, apply one fix (code split, animation discipline, resource hints, or caching), and re-measure. Write it as a case study: baseline vitals, diagnosis, fix, after-numbers. Deliverable: the case study — the artifact that turns 'I know performance' into 'here's the proof.'

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: performance numbers are device- and network-specific — a fix that wins on a flagship phone may not move a budget device, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers score the method (profile, fix, re-measure); absolute numbers are context, not truth.

notes.title: Worked example: prefetch differs from preload in that:
notes.body:
**Problem.** prefetch differs from preload in that:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** prefetch is low-priority for likely-future navigations; preload is high-priority for the current page
- **Why:** Priority and intent differ: current-page critical vs next-navigation likely.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Priority and intent differ: current-page critical vs next-navigation likely.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In Browser Rendering and Performance, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in Browser Rendering and Performance gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

cards.front: Box model and specificity in 30 seconds?
cards.back: Content + padding + border + margin; box-sizing: border-box makes widths sane. Specificity: inline > ID > class > element; the cascade resolves ties by source order. Keep specificity flat (BEM/utilities) so overrides stay predictable.

cards.front: Flexbox vs Grid: the choosing rule?
cards.back: Flexbox for one-dimensional layout (a row or column of items, content-driven sizing). Grid for two-dimensional layout (rows AND columns, explicit placement). Most real UIs compose both.

cards.front: How do you discuss responsive design modernly?
cards.back: Fluid layouts + breakpoints for viewport adaptation, container queries for component-level responsiveness (the component adapts to its container, not the viewport). The interview line: ‘viewport queries adapt pages; container queries adapt components.’

cards.front: How do you keep CSS maintainable at scale?
cards.back: Architecture with flat specificity: BEM naming (block__element--modifier), CSS modules for scoping, or utility classes — pick one and enforce it. The interview line: ‘specificity wars are a process failure, not a CSS failure.’

cards.front: What’s the transform-and-opacity discipline?
cards.back: Animate only transform and opacity: they composite on the GPU without layout or paint. Animating width/left/top triggers reflow — jank. The interview line: ‘if it moves pixels through layout, it’s not an animation, it’s a slideshow.’

cards.front: How do you explain stacking contexts?
cards.back: z-index only competes within a stacking context — created by positioned elements with z-index, opacity below 1, transforms, and others. The interview line: ‘z-index is local, not global — find the context.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in container queries?
cards.back: Components responding to their container’s size instead of the viewport’s — true component-level responsiveness. The interview line: ‘container queries let the component own its breakpoints.’

cards.front: How do you discuss CSS performance?
cards.back: Selectors are cheap; layout and paint are expensive — contain layout with content-visibility, avoid animating layout properties, keep the DOM shallow. The interview line: ‘CSS performance is about what you ask the browser to recompute.’

cards.front: Using a <div> with onClick instead of <button> harms accessibility because:
cards.back: **It loses built-in keyboard support, focus, and screen-reader semantics** — Native controls carry keyboard handling and ARIA roles for free; divs need all of it rebuilt.

cards.front: A janky animation’s usual cause is:
cards.back: **Animating layout-triggering properties instead of transform/opacity** — Layout per frame blows the 16ms budget; composited properties don’t.

cards.front: BEM’s naming discipline prevents:
cards.back: **Specificity wars — flat, predictable selectors instead of deep nesting** — block__element--modifier keeps every selector at one class of specificity: overrides stay sane.

cards.front: Container queries improve on media queries by:
cards.back: **Letting components respond to their container’s size — reusable in any layout** — Component-level responsiveness: the same card works in a sidebar and a full page.

cards.back: Requirements (post, follow, ranked feed), API, data model (posts, edges), fan-out: push for normal users, pull for celebrities (the famous hybrid), ranking separate from delivery, cache hot feeds, pagination.

cards.front: Design typeahead/autocomplete: the key decisions?
cards.back: Debounce input (~200–300ms), prefix index (trie or indexed prefix column), rank by popularity/recency, cache hot prefixes aggressively. Client: cancel stale in-flight requests so slow responses don’t overwrite fresh ones.

cards.front: How do you design a photo gallery at scale?
cards.back: Upload → object storage → async thumbnails (multiple sizes) → CDN in front → lazy loading + responsive images (srcset) on the client. The interview line: ‘bytes are the budget — every decision serves fewer, smaller, closer bytes.’

cards.front: How do you handle client-side caching and state sync?
cards.back: Normalize server data in a client cache (React Query/SWR style): stale-while-revalidate for freshness, cache keys as query keys, optimistic updates with rollback on error, and invalidation tied to mutations. The interview line: ‘the server is the truth; the client cache is a performance layer with an eviction policy.’

cards.front: Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets?
cards.back: Polling: simple, wasteful (empty responses). SSE: server→client stream over HTTP, auto-reconnect — perfect for notifications/feeds. WebSockets: full duplex — chat, games, collaboration. Choose the weakest tool that satisfies the direction and frequency.

cards.front: How do you design a collaborative editor’s frontend?
cards.back: Local-first state with operational transforms or CRDTs for convergence, presence over WebSockets, and the server as the ordering authority. The interview line: ‘collaboration is conflict resolution with a UI.’

cards.front: What are the key decisions in a design-a-dashboard answer?
cards.back: Data freshness requirements (real-time vs periodic), virtualization for large lists, and the charting and rendering budget — then the API shape that serves it (aggregations server-side). The interview line: ‘dashboards are won or lost on the data contract.’

cards.front: How do you handle offline in a frontend system design?
cards.back: Service worker caching strategies (cache-first for the app shell, network-first for data), queued mutations with sync on reconnect, and conflict UI. The interview line: ‘offline is a state, not an error — design the queue.’

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **News-feed fan-out** — Push for normal users, pull for celebrities — the famous hybrid; ranking separated from delivery, hot feeds cached, paginated.
- **Typeahead design** — Debounced input (~200–300ms), prefix index (trie or indexed prefix column), popularity/recency ranking, aggressive caching of hot prefixes — plus canceling stale in-flight requests client-side.
- **Photo pipeline** — Upload → object storage → async thumbnails (multiple sizes) → CDN → lazy loading + responsive images (srcset): 'bytes are the budget.'
- **Client cache (SWR-style)** — Normalized server data with stale-while-revalidate: instant render from cache, fresh data moments later — invalidation tied to mutations.
- **Optimistic updates** — Apply the mutation to UI immediately, roll back on server rejection — the UX bet with the hedge built in.
- **Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets** — Polling: simple, wasteful. SSE: server→client stream with auto-reconnect — feeds and notifications. WebSockets: full duplex — chat, games, collaboration. Weakest tool that satisfies direction and frequency.
- **State sync** — Server as truth, client cache as a performance layer allowed to be briefly wrong, never permanently wrong.
- **Frontend walkthrough** — Requirements → component tree and data flow → API → caching/sync → rendering perf → real-time — the client-side shape of the standard walkthrough.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Whiteboard the news feed in 45 minutes: requirements, API, data model, fan-out decision with the celebrity math, caching, pagination — narrate tradeoffs throughout.
2. Design typeahead end to end: debounce timing, prefix index choice, ranking inputs, cache layers, and the stale-request cancellation on the client.
3. Design the photo gallery: upload flow, thumbnail sizes, CDN placement, lazy loading and srcset strategy — with the byte budget stated.
4. Choose the real-time mechanism for three features (notifications, chat, live dashboard): name direction and frequency, pick the weakest sufficient tool, state the rejected options.
5. Draw one client architecture (state, cache/sync, rendering, real-time) and present it in 10 minutes — the frontend design-round compressed rep.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Frontend design portfolio. Write two one-page design docs — the news feed and one more (typeahead or photo gallery) — each with requirements, component tree and data flow, API, caching/sync strategy, rendering-perf plan, and real-time choice. Record a 20-minute walkthrough of one. Deliverable: two docs plus the recording — the client-side design evidence.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: frontend design rounds are the least standardized interviews in the loop — expectations swing widely by company, and this course confers no certificate. The walkthrough is a communication skill; the 'right' architecture always depends on the product's actual constraints.

notes.title: Worked example: A frontend design round emphasizes:
notes.body:
**Problem.** A frontend design round emphasizes:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Client architecture: state, caching/sync, rendering perf, real-time
- **Why:** The graded system is the client: how it manages state, data, and performance at scale.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *The graded system is the client: how it manages state, data, and performance at scale.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In Frontend System Design, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in Frontend System Design gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

cards.front: What accessibility points score in frontend interviews?
cards.back: Semantic HTML first (buttons are <button>), visible focus states, color contrast, labels for inputs, alt text that conveys function, and keyboard operability. The line: ‘accessibility is a correctness requirement, tested like any other.’

cards.front: How do you approach a Kanban-with-drag-and-drop machine-coding task?
cards.back: Data model first (columns → cards, normalized), HTML5 drag events or pointer events, optimistic state updates with keyboard-accessible fallback, and clean component APIs. The interview line: ‘the data model is the app — drag-and-drop is just the input method.’

cards.front: How do you win a machine-coding round?
cards.back: The 90-minute cadence: 10 min clarify + plan the component API, 60 min build working-first (happy path before polish), 20 min edge cases + tests. Clean props interfaces matter more than pixel perfection — interviewers read your API design.

cards.front: How do you test a machine-coding build?
cards.back: Testing Library philosophy: test user-visible behavior (roles, text), not implementation details. Happy path + key edge cases (empty states, errors), accessible queries as a bonus a11y check. The interview line: ‘my tests describe what the user can do.’

cards.front: How do you scope a machine-coding task in the first ten minutes?
cards.back: Restate the requirements, enumerate the components and their props or events, and name what you will NOT build. The interview line: ‘a scoped plan is half the score — the rest is execution.’

cards.front: How do you structure state in a machine-coding build?
cards.back: One normalized store for the domain data (columns map to card maps), derived state computed at render, and UI-only state kept local. The interview line: ‘normalize the data, derive the rest.’

cards.front: What separates a passing machine-coding submission from a strong one?
cards.back: Working happy path first, then edge cases (empty states, loading, errors), then polish (keyboard support, focus management). The interview line: ‘correct, then robust, then delightful — in that order.’

cards.front: Testing Library prefers role-based queries because:
cards.back: **They test the accessible experience — the test breaks when accessibility breaks** — Querying by role aligns tests with how users (and assistive tech) find elements.

cards.front: In machine coding, ‘working first’ means:
cards.back: **Happy path functional before polish and edge cases — a demoable build beats a perfect fragment** — Interviewers score a working build with clean APIs; polish without function scores nothing.

cards.front: Keyboard-accessible drag-and-drop matters because:
cards.back: **Pointer-only interaction excludes keyboard users — accessibility is a correctness requirement** — Every pointer interaction needs a keyboard equivalent; interviewers check.

cards.front: Using a <div> with onClick instead of <button> harms accessibility because:
cards.back: **It loses built-in keyboard support, focus, and screen-reader semantics** — Native controls carry keyboard handling and ARIA roles for free; divs need all of it rebuilt.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure

Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Build the typeahead in 90 minutes on a timer: 10 plan the component API, 60 working-first, 20 edge cases + tests — then score yourself on API cleanliness.
2. Build the accessible carousel in 90 minutes: keyboard operable, focus visible, slide changes announced — test it keyboard-only at the end.
3. Build the Kanban in 90 minutes: normalized data model first, drag-and-drop second, keyboard fallback third — narrate the API choices as you go.
4. Write Testing Library tests for one build: happy path plus two edge cases, role-based queries only — verify the tests break when accessibility breaks.
5. Review all three builds against the rubric: working-first? clean APIs? tests? accessibility? — log the pattern in your misses.

cards.front: What’s a behavioral ledger?
cards.back: Your running record: story bank entries, which stories you’ve told where, feedback received, and follow-up questions that stumped you. It stops you from repeating the same story and turns each behavioral round into training data.

cards.front: How do you debrief and triage after a mock?

cards.front: Walk the request path: DNS to render.
cards.back: DNS resolve → TCP handshake → TLS → request hits CDN/edge → load balancer → app server → (cache → DB) → response → browser parses HTML/CSS/JS → render. Saying the full path out loud is the fullstack flex — then zoom into wherever the question points.

cards.front: Monolith vs modular monolith vs microservices?
cards.back: Monolith: one deployable, simplest ops. Modular monolith: bounded-context modules inside one deployable — the discipline without the distributed tax. Microservices: independent deployables — pay the distributed-systems cost only when seams demand it. The interview line: ‘I evolve toward distribution, I don’t start there.’

cards.front: What’s the BFF pattern?
cards.back: Backend-for-Frontend: a thin service per client type (web, mobile) that aggregates downstream microservices into exactly the shapes each UI needs — killing over-fetching without leaking service topology to clients.

cards.front: SSR vs SSG vs ISR?
cards.back: SSR: render per request (fresh, slower TTFB). SSG: render at build (fastest, stale until rebuild). ISR: static with timed revalidation (the middle path). Choose by freshness needs: marketing page → SSG; personalized dashboard → SSR.

cards.front: How do you reason about edge and CDN placement?
cards.back: Push static and cacheable dynamic content to the edge (CDN PoPs), compute at the edge only when latency demands it (edge functions), origin for the source of truth. The interview line: ‘every mile between the user and the byte is latency I can buy off.’

cards.front: How do you discuss the modular monolith honestly?
cards.back: Bounded-context modules inside one deployable: most of microservices’ organization benefits, none of the network failure modes — with a clean seam for extracting services later. The interview line: ‘the modular monolith is the default; microservices are the opt-in.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in request hedging and timeouts?
cards.back: Timeouts with budgets per hop (not one global timeout), hedged requests for tail latency, and circuit breakers to stop cascading. The interview line: ‘timeouts are a design decision, not a config value.’

cards.front: How do you reason about data gravity in fullstack design?
cards.back: Compute moves toward the data, not the reverse: colocate app servers with the database region, push only aggregates to the edge. The interview line: ‘bandwidth bills follow data movement — minimize the movement.’

cards.front: Drawing before diving deep is strong because:
cards.back: **It establishes shared context — then both of you know where the deep dive lives** — The diagram is the map; deep dives are the territory. Maps first.

cards.front: Edge computing earns its keep when:
cards.back: **Latency is the constraint and the work is cacheable or lightweight per request** — Edge pays for latency-sensitive, lightweight work — not for heavy computation.

cards.front: ISR’s advantage over pure SSG is:
cards.back: **Pages revalidate in the background on an interval — fresh without rebuilds** — Stale-while-revalidate at the page level: serve cached, regenerate on schedule.

cards.front: A BFF mainly solves:
cards.back: **Over/under-fetching by shaping responses per client** — Each client gets an aggregation layer tuned to its screens instead of N chatty service calls.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Request path** — DNS → TCP → TLS → CDN/edge → load balancer → app server → (cache → DB) → response → parse → render — saying the full path aloud is the fullstack flex.
- **Monolith** — One deployable, simplest ops — the honest starting point until a seam proves otherwise.
- **Modular monolith** — Bounded-context modules inside one deployable — the discipline without the distributed tax.
- **Microservices** — Independent deployables — the distributed-systems cost paid only when proven seams demand it.
- **BFF** — Backend-for-Frontend: a thin service per client type aggregating downstream services into exactly the shapes each UI needs — killing over-fetching without leaking topology.
- **SSR** — Render per request: fresh, slower TTFB — personalized dashboards, authenticated content.
- **SSG** — Render at build: fastest, stale until rebuild — marketing pages, docs.
- **ISR** — Static with timed revalidation: fresh without rebuilds — the middle path for mostly-static content that changes.
- **Edge placement** — Static and cacheable dynamic content at CDN PoPs; compute at the edge only when latency demands it; origin as the source of truth.
- **Draw-before-dive** — Establishing shared context first — then both you and the interviewer know where the deep dive lives.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Draw the full request path for an app you know, hop by hop, from DNS to render — then narrate it aloud in under three minutes.
2. For one product, choose the architecture: monolith, modular monolith, or services — write the seam analysis that justifies the call and the condition that would flip it.
3. Decide the rendering strategy per page of a sample site (landing, dashboard, docs, feed): SSG, SSR, or ISR — with the freshness argument for each.
4. Place the edge: mark on your request-path diagram what lives at the CDN, what computes at the edge, and what stays at the origin — with the latency argument per placement.
5. Present the whole-path diagram in 10 minutes to a partner: map first, then one deep dive where they point — practice the draw-before-dive discipline.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Whole-path architecture brief. For a product you choose: the request-path diagram with every hop labeled, the architecture decision (monolith → services spectrum) with the seam analysis, per-page rendering strategy with freshness arguments, and the edge-placement map. Deliverable: the brief — the artifact you will adapt live when a fullstack loop asks you to 'design the whole thing.'

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: 'fullstack' depth is breadth by design — no one is expert at every hop, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers test whether you can reason across the path and know where your depth ends; claiming depth everywhere is the fastest way to lose credibility.

notes.title: Worked example: Drawing before diving deep is strong because:
notes.body:
**Problem.** Drawing before diving deep is strong because:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** It establishes shared context — then both of you know where the deep dive lives
- **Why:** The diagram is the map; deep dives are the territory. Maps first.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *The diagram is the map; deep dives are the territory.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In Fullstack Architecture, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in Fullstack Architecture gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

cards.front: What makes an API ‘RESTful’ in an interview answer?
cards.back: Resources as nouns in URLs, HTTP verbs as actions, status codes as the contract (200/201/400/401/403/404/429/500), stateless requests, and versioning — then the judgment calls: pagination, filtering, and idempotency.

cards.front: When do queries beat endpoints — your GraphQL judgment call?
cards.back: When clients need varied, nested data and over/under-fetching hurts (mobile, aggregations): one query, exact fields, typed schema. The costs you must name: caching is harder, query complexity needs limits, and N+1 resolvers need batching (dataloaders).

cards.front: Over-fetching vs under-fetching — the honest comparison?
cards.back: Over-fetching: REST endpoints returning fields the client ignores (wasted bytes). Under-fetching: needing N requests for one screen (chatty). GraphQL fixes both per-query; the cost is caching complexity. The interview line: ‘I measure the waste before I prescribe the cure.’

cards.front: How do you discuss caching with GraphQL?
cards.back: Harder than REST because POST-to-one-endpoint defeats HTTP caching: the answers are normalized client caches (Apollo-style, keyed by type + id), persisted queries for CDN caching, and server-side dataloader batching to kill N+1. The interview line: ‘GraphQL moves caching from the network layer into the client.’

cards.front: Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets?
cards.back: Polling: simple, wasteful (empty responses). SSE: server→client stream over HTTP, auto-reconnect — perfect for notifications/feeds. WebSockets: full duplex — chat, games, collaboration. Choose the weakest tool that satisfies the direction and frequency.

cards.front: How do you discuss schema design in GraphQL interviews?
cards.back: Types that mirror the domain, connections for pagination (edges, nodes, pageInfo), and mutations that return the changed object for cache updates. The interview line: ‘the schema is the API’s type system — design it like one.’

cards.front: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL specifically?
cards.back: One resolver query per parent object — the classic nested-list explosion. The fix is dataloader-style batching: collect keys per tick, fetch once. The interview line: ‘GraphQL makes N+1 easy to write and dataloader makes it easy to fix.’

cards.front: When do you choose REST over GraphQL in an interview?
cards.back: When HTTP caching matters (CDNs, intermediaries), when the API is simple CRUD, or when clients are few and known. The interview line: ‘GraphQL optimizes for client flexibility; REST optimizes for the network.’

cards.front: Per-surface API choice is justified because:
cards.back: **Client constraints differ (bandwidth, latency, capabilities) — the contract should fit the consumer** — The consumer’s constraints decide the contract shape, not architectural purity.

cards.front: Server-Sent Events fit a live notification feed because:
cards.back: **They’re a simple server-to-client stream with auto-reconnect — exactly the direction needed** — One-directional updates over plain HTTP: less machinery than WebSockets for the same job.

cards.front: Every caching decision must name:
cards.back: **The invalidation strategy — stale data is caching’s permanent tax** — Cache without an invalidation story is a future incident.

cards.front: Under-fetching hurts mobile clients most because:
cards.back: **Many sequential round trips compound on high-latency networks** — Chatty APIs multiply round-trip latency — the scarcest resource on mobile networks.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **REST resource modeling** — Resources as nouns, verbs as actions, status codes as the contract — the cacheable, toolable default.
- **GraphQL schema** — Types, queries, mutations: the typed contract clients shape per request — exact fields, one round trip.
- **Over-fetching** — REST endpoints returning fields the client ignores — wasted bytes, the cost GraphQL eliminates.
- **Under-fetching** — Needing N requests for one screen — chatty on high-latency networks, the cost GraphQL eliminates.
- **GraphQL caching cost** — A single endpoint with arbitrary query shapes defeats HTTP caching and simple per-route limits — the price of client-shaped queries; query-cost analysis required.
- **N+1 resolvers** — Per-field resolvers firing per row — the GraphQL performance trap, fixed by batching (dataloaders).
- **Subscriptions** — GraphQL's real-time primitive — server-pushed updates over a persistent connection for live data.
- **Per-surface choice** — Client constraints (bandwidth, latency, capabilities) decide the contract shape — not architectural purity.
- **Caching as a tradeoff** — What to cache, where, the invalidation strategy, the failure story — 'caching is a tradeoff with an invalidation plan, not a speedup.'
- **Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets** — Polling: simple, wasteful. SSE: server→client stream, auto-reconnect. WebSockets: full duplex — weakest sufficient tool per direction and frequency.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:

1. Model one screen's data needs twice: as REST endpoints (count the requests and wasted fields) and as one GraphQL query — write the over/under-fetching ledger for both.
2. Write the caching plan for the REST version (HTTP cache semantics, CDN, invalidation) and then for the GraphQL version (query hashing, persisted queries, cost limits) — compare the machinery.
3. Diagnose an N+1 resolver scenario on paper: per-row field resolvers, the query count explosion, then the dataloader batching fix — state the before/after query counts.
4. Choose the real-time mechanism for three features (notifications, chat, live dashboard): direction, frequency, weakest sufficient tool — with the rejected options named.
5. Argue one per-surface decision aloud in two minutes: 'mobile feed → GraphQL because…, public API → REST because…' — verdict plus the flip condition.

cards.front: Sessions vs tokens?
cards.back: Sessions: server-side state keyed by cookie — revocable instantly, needs sticky/shared store at scale. Tokens (JWT): stateless, self-contained — scales horizontally, but revocation needs denylists/short expiry. Choose by revocation needs.

cards.front: What’s inside a JWT, and what must you validate?
cards.back: Header.payload.signature, base64url: claims like sub, exp, iat. Validate: signature with the right key/algorithm (never ‘none’), expiry, issuer/audience. And the warning: JWTs are signed, not encrypted — never put secrets in claims.

cards.front: Walk the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.
cards.back: User → client redirects to auth server → user approves → auth code returned → client exchanges code (+ secret, PKCE for public clients) for tokens at the token endpoint. The code is short-lived and single-use; tokens never touch the browser URL.

cards.front: How do you store passwords — the interview answer?
cards.back: Never encrypt (reversible); hash with a memory-hard, salted function: Argon2id preferred, bcrypt acceptable. Per-user random salt, work factor tuned so login takes ~hundreds of ms. And never roll your own crypto.

cards.front: Which auth questions decide senior loops?
cards.back: ‘How do you revoke a JWT?’ (short expiry + denylist/rotation), ‘where do refresh tokens live?’ (httpOnly secure cookies, rotated), ‘how do you do SSO?’ (OIDC). The interview line: ‘I answer auth with threat models, not library names.’

cards.front: How do you explain refresh token rotation?
cards.back: Short-lived access tokens plus rotating refresh tokens: each use issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old, so a stolen token has a short window and reuse is detectable. The interview line: ‘rotation turns theft into an alarm.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in multi-tenancy auth?
cards.back: Tenant isolation at the data layer (tenant_id on every query or schema-per-tenant), token claims carrying the tenant, and admin scoping that cannot cross tenants. The interview line: ‘the tenant boundary is the security boundary.’

cards.front: How do you discuss passkeys in an interview?
cards.back: Phishing-resistant public-key credentials synced by the platform: no shared secret to phish or leak, with fallback for account recovery as the hard part. The interview line: ‘passkeys remove the password without removing the recovery problem.’

cards.front: JWT revocation’s honest answer is:

cards.front: Passwords must be hashed, not encrypted, because:
cards.back: **Encryption is reversible — a key leak exposes every password; hashing is one-way** — One-way hashing means even a full database theft doesn’t yield passwords (beyond cracking).

cards.front: PKCE exists to protect:
cards.back: **Public clients (mobile/SPA) that can’t keep a secret — the code exchange is bound to the original request** — Without a client secret, PKCE’s code_verifier/code_challenge pair prevents authorization-code interception.

cards.front: A JWT is ___ not ___:
cards.back: **Signed; encrypted** — Anyone can read the payload; the signature only proves it wasn’t tampered with.
