notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Sessions** — Server-side state keyed by cookie — revocable instantly, needs a shared store at scale; the stateful default.
- **Tokens (JWT)** — Stateless, self-contained — scales horizontally, but revocation needs denylists or short expiry; the stateless tradeoff.
- **JWT structure** — header.payload.signature, base64url — claims like sub, exp, iat; signed, not encrypted: never put secrets in claims.
- **JWT validation** — Signature with the right key and algorithm (never 'none'), expiry, issuer, audience — every one checked, every time.
- **OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow** — User → client redirects to auth server → approval → short-lived single-use code → code (+ secret, PKCE for public clients) exchanged for tokens; tokens never touch the browser URL.
- **PKCE** — code_verifier/code_challenge pair protecting public clients (mobile/SPA) that can't keep a secret — prevents authorization-code interception.
- **OpenID Connect** — The identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0: standardized ID tokens for 'who is this user' — SSO's building block.
- **Password hashing** — Never encrypt (reversible) — hash with a memory-hard salted function: Argon2id preferred, bcrypt acceptable; per-user salt; work factor tuned so login takes hundreds of milliseconds.
- **Refresh token storage** — httpOnly secure cookies, rotated on use — the answer to 'where do refresh tokens live.'
- **JWT revocation** — The honest answer: short-lived access tokens plus refresh-token rotation and denylists — statelessness means bounding the exposure window, not central killing.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Draw the authorization code flow with PKCE end to end: every redirect, the code exchange, where each token lives — then narrate it aloud in three minutes.
2. Write the JWT validation checklist for a resource server: algorithm, signature key, exp, iss, aud — then list what breaks if each check is skipped.
3. Compare sessions vs tokens for two products (a bank dashboard, a content API): revocation needs, scale needs, the verdict per product with reasons.
4. Write the password-storage spec: algorithm choice, salt strategy, work-factor target, and the 'never roll your own crypto' rule — as you'd state it in an interview.
5. Answer the three senior-loop auth questions aloud: 'how do you revoke a JWT?', 'where do refresh tokens live?', 'how do you do SSO?' — threat model first, mechanism second.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Auth design brief. For a two-client product: the flow choice (sessions vs tokens, with the revocation analysis), the OAuth/OIDC integration sketch, the JWT validation checklist, refresh-token storage and rotation policy, and the password-hashing spec. Include the threat model: what each decision defends against. Deliverable: the brief — auth argued from threat models.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: auth is the topic where overconfidence is dangerous — real systems add key rotation, breach response, and compliance that interviews skip, and this course confers no certificate. State the threat model honestly; 'it depends on the threat model' is a senior answer, not evasion.

notes.title: Worked example: JWT revocation’s honest answer is:
notes.body:
**Problem.** JWT revocation’s honest answer is:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Short-lived access tokens + refresh-token rotation and denylists — statelessness has a revocation cost
- **Why:** Stateless tokens can’t be centrally killed; the design bounds the exposure window instead.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Stateless tokens can’t be centrally killed; the design bounds the exposure window instead.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In Auth and Identity, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in Auth and Identity gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

modules.summary: Welcome to Auth and Identity — module 3 of the Fullstack path. I'm your instructor, and this is auth without hand-waving: the flows, the token lifecycle, and the storage decisions — the topic where bluffing is most visible and most punished. We cover sessions versus tokens, JWT structure and validation, the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, OpenID Connect on top, and password hashing with bcrypt and Argon2. By the end, you will answer auth with threat models, not library names.

cards.front: ORMs vs query builders vs raw SQL?
cards.back: ORMs: speed of development, relationships as objects — watch N+1 and leaky abstraction on complex queries. Query builders: composable SQL without string soup. Raw SQL: full control for reporting/analytics. The senior line: ‘I use the ORM for CRUD and drop to SQL where it earns it.’

cards.front: How do you discuss full-text search basics?
cards.back: Inverted index: terms → documents, with tokenization, stemming, and ranking (TF-IDF/BM25). For interview depth: Postgres tsvector covers the simple case; dedicated engines (OpenSearch/Elasticsearch) earn their keep at scale, faceting, and relevance tuning.

cards.front: How do you handle file uploads at scale?
cards.back: Direct-to-object-storage uploads (presigned URLs — the app server never proxies bytes), async processing (thumbnails, virus scan) via queues, CDN in front for reads. The interview line: ‘bytes never touch my app servers.’

cards.front: How do you keep client cache and DB consistent?
cards.back: Server as source of truth; client cache as a performance layer with invalidation tied to mutations (optimistic updates + rollback on error, or refetch-on-mutation). The interview line: ‘the client cache is allowed to be wrong briefly, never permanently.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'From form to row: validation layers'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: How do you discuss event-driven data flow across the stack?
cards.back: Domain events from the write side feed read models, search indexes, and notifications — each consumer independent, each replayable. The interview line: ‘events decouple the write model from every read model.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in pagination at scale?
cards.back: Cursor-based (stable under inserts), keyset on indexed columns, and the total-count problem (expensive — estimate or drop it). The interview line: ‘deep pages are a database problem wearing a UI costume.’

cards.front: How do you talk about data validation layers?
cards.back: Client for UX speed, API boundary as the trust boundary (never trust the client), database constraints as the last line. The interview line: ‘validate everywhere, trust the server’s validation.’

cards.front: Optimistic updates need a rollback path because:
cards.back: **The server can reject the mutation — the UI must revert to truth** — Optimism is a UX bet; the rollback is the hedge when the bet loses.

cards.front: Presigned URLs for uploads are preferred because:
cards.back: **Clients upload straight to object storage — app servers never proxy the bytes** — Offloading byte transfer removes the app tier from the bandwidth path entirely.

cards.front: An inverted index maps:
cards.back: **Terms to the documents containing them — enabling fast keyword lookup** — Search flips the document: instead of scanning text, you look up precomputed term postings.

cards.front: An ORM’s classic performance trap is:
cards.back: **N+1 queries from lazy-loaded relationships in loops** — Accessing relations per-row in a loop fires a query each — eager loading is the fix.

cards.front: What does a good CI/CD pipeline do?
cards.back: CI: every push builds, lints, tests, scans — fast feedback on main. CD: artifacts promoted through environments, deployments automated (blue-green/canary/rolling), rollback one command. The interview metrics: lead time and change-failure rate.

cards.front: Why do fullstack interviews love feature flags?
cards.back: They decouple deploy from release: merge dark code, release to 1%, kill-switch bad launches without redeploying. The discipline to name: flag hygiene — every flag gets an owner and a removal date, or you inherit flag spaghetti.

cards.front: What does Docker actually give you?
cards.back: A portable, reproducible runtime: the image bundles code + dependencies + OS userland, so ‘works on my machine’ dies. Containers share the host kernel (lighter than VMs, weaker isolation) — and the interview follow-up is always about image size and layer caching.

cards.front: Logs, metrics, traces — when do you reach for each?
cards.back: Metrics: ‘is something wrong’ (alerts, dashboards). Logs: ‘what happened’ (discrete events with context). Traces: ‘where did the request go’ (latency across services). The interview line: ‘metrics alert me, traces show me where, logs tell me why.’

cards.front: What’s a real rollback strategy?
cards.back: Deploy immutable artifacts, keep the previous version one command away (or N−1 running in blue-green), database migrations backward-compatible (expand-contract), and rehearse the rollback — an untested rollback plan is a hope.

cards.front: How do you explain blue-green deployments in an interview?
cards.back: Two identical environments: deploy to idle (green), smoke-test, flip the router, keep blue warm for instant rollback. Costs double capacity during the switch. The interview line: ‘blue-green trades capacity for rollback certainty.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in infrastructure as code basics?
cards.back: Declarative desired state, plan-before-apply review, and remote state with locking — the pipeline deploys the infrastructure like code. The interview line: ‘if it is not in code, it does not exist.’

cards.front: How do you discuss secrets in deployment interviews?
cards.back: Never in repos or images: injected at deploy time from a secret manager, rotated on a schedule, and scoped per environment. The interview line: ‘a secret in git is a secret shared with the world.’

cards.front: Blue-green deployment’s rollback is:
cards.back: **Instant: flip the router back to the still-running green environment** — The old environment stays live behind the router until cutover is verified — rollback is a route change.

cards.front: A distributed trace’s primary value is:
cards.back: **Following one request across services to find where latency/errors originate** — Trace spans stitch the request path across service boundaries — the only view that crosses them.

cards.front: Containers differ from VMs in that they:
cards.back: **Share the host OS kernel instead of virtualizing hardware** — No guest kernel per container: faster startup, denser packing, but a shared kernel attack surface.

cards.front: Feature flags decouple:
cards.back: **Deploying code from releasing features to users** — Code ships dark; the flag controls who sees it — enabling progressive rollout and instant kill-switches.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **CI** — Every push builds, lints, tests, scans — fast feedback on main; the definition of done, enforced mechanically.
- **CD** — Artifacts promoted through environments with automated deployments (blue-green/canary/rolling) and one-command rollback — lead time and change-failure rate as the metrics.
- **Feature flags** — Decouple deploy from release: merge dark, release to 1%, kill-switch without redeploying — with flag hygiene (owner + removal date) or flag spaghetti.
- **Environments** — Dev → staging → production with promotion discipline — staging that mirrors production is the point, not the checkbox.
- **Docker** — Portable, reproducible runtime: image bundles code + dependencies + OS userland — containers share the host kernel (lighter than VMs, weaker isolation).
- **Blue-green rollback** — Instant: flip the router back to the still-running previous environment — rollback as a route change, rehearsed not hoped.
- **Observability trio** — Metrics alert, traces show where, logs tell why — 'metrics alert me, traces show me where, logs tell me why.'
- **Rollback rehearsal** — Immutable artifacts, previous version one command away, backward-compatible migrations — an untested rollback plan is a hope.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Sketch the CI/CD pipeline for your capstone: triggers, parallel jobs (lint/test/build/scan), artifact promotion, environments — with the gate that blocks a bad merge.
2. Write the feature-flag plan for one risky launch: flag name, owner, rollout percentages, kill-switch procedure, removal date — the hygiene, not just the flag.
3. Containerize a toy app: write the Dockerfile, note the layer-caching order, shrink the image — then state what Docker did and didn't give you versus a VM.
4. Design the rollback for one deploy: immutable artifact, blue-green or canary, the router flip, the migration-compatibility check — then rehearse it on paper.
5. Write the observability starter set: three alerting metrics, what each log line carries, where you'd add the first trace — the owner's minimum.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Deployment runbook. For your capstone app: the CI/CD pipeline definition, environment promotion rules, the feature-flag register (with owners and removal dates), the container strategy, and the rollback runbook — including the migration-compatibility rule and the rehearsal log. Deliverable: the runbook — deployment literacy written down.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: 'deployment literacy' is literacy, not operations expertise — real on-call involves incidents, cost, and compliance this module doesn't simulate, and this course confers no certificate. The interview tests whether you think like an owner; the pager teaches the rest.

notes.title: Worked example: Blue-green deployment’s rollback is:
notes.body:
**Problem.** Blue-green deployment’s rollback is:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Instant: flip the router back to the still-running green environment
- **Why:** The old environment stays live behind the router until cutover is verified — rollback is a route change.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *The old environment stays live behind the router until cutover is verified — rollback is a route change.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In Deployment Literacy, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in Deployment Literacy gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

cards.back: Thinnest slice that demonstrates the skill: API contract first, auth + data model, deployed with CI, README and demo script. The interview line: ‘shipped and demoable beats ambitious and half-built.’

cards.front: What goes in an API contract / OpenAPI sketch?
cards.back: Endpoints, methods, request/response schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits, and versioning — enough that a client team could build against it. The interview line: ‘the contract is the interface; code is the implementation.’

cards.front: What makes a capstone README and demo script work?
cards.back: README: what it does, how to run it, architecture in one diagram, decisions and tradeoffs. Demo script: the 3-minute happy path with one ‘and here’s the interesting part’ beat. The interview line: ‘the README is the interview before the interview.’

cards.front: How do you present a build in an interview?
cards.back: Live demo of the happy path, then the architecture (one diagram), then the two hardest decisions with alternatives, then ‘what I’d do with more time.’ The interview line: ‘demo the value, narrate the judgment.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Scoping a shippable app'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: How do you choose a capstone that scores in interviews?
cards.back: One hard problem done well beats three toy apps: pick something with a real data model, auth, and a deployed URL — the trifecta interviewers actually click. The interview line: ‘depth in one project beats breadth in five.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in your capstone’s tradeoff story?
cards.back: Why this stack, what you rejected and why, and what broke during the build. The interview line: ‘the capstone is an excuse to tell decision stories.’

cards.front: How do you keep a capstone honest about AI assistance?
cards.back: Disclose the tooling, own every line (be ready to explain and modify any of it live), and keep the architecture decisions visibly yours. The interview line: ‘assistance is fine; authorship you cannot defend is not.’

cards.front: Ending with ‘what I’d do with more time’ is strong because:
cards.back: **It shows you see the work’s limits and can prioritize — a senior signal** — Named next steps prove the build was scoped deliberately, not abandoned.

cards.front: An architecture diagram in the README is worth it because:
cards.back: **Reviewers grasp the system in 30 seconds — before reading a line of code** — Hiring managers skim; the diagram carries the design when they won’t read prose.

cards.front: Writing the contract before the implementation is strong because:
cards.back: **It forces interface decisions early, when they’re cheap — and enables parallel client/server work** — Contract-first surfaces disagreements before code cements them.

cards.front: API-contract-first in a capstone is strong because:
cards.back: **It proves interface thinking and lets frontend/backend evolve independently** — Contracts before code: the habit interviewers want to see generalized.

- **Contract-first** — Interface decisions early when they're cheap — frontend and backend evolve independently against the contract.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Scope the capstone in one page: the thinnest shippable slice, the explicit non-goals, the contract-first order of work — get the scope signed off (by a peer or yourself, in writing).
2. Write the API contract before any code: endpoints, schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits — the interface the build must satisfy.
3. Build vertical slices: auth + one full feature path end to end (UI → API → DB → deploy) before adding breadth — demoable at every commit.
4. Wire CI on day one: every push builds and tests, deploys gated — the pipeline grows with the app, not after it.
5. Write the README and demo script, then present: live demo, one architecture diagram, two hardest decisions, 'what I'd do with more time' — record it.

cards.front: How do you handle full-stack live rounds (design + coding)?
cards.back: Timebox visibly: design the path first (10 min), then code the thinnest vertical slice (API + one screen), narrating tradeoffs. The interview line: ‘I’d rather demo a thin working slice than describe a thick imaginary one.’

cards.front: How do you handle timed API-design rounds?
cards.back: Budget: 5 min requirements, 10 min resources + verbs + status codes, 10 min edge cases (pagination, idempotency, versioning), 5 min tradeoffs. Think in resources and contracts — the interview line: ‘I design the contract a client could program against.’

cards.front: What’s a behavioral ledger?
cards.back: Your running record: story bank entries, which stories you’ve told where, feedback received, and follow-up questions that stumped you. It stops you from repeating the same story and turns each behavioral round into training data.

cards.front: How do you debrief and triage after a mock?
cards.back: Within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), rank leaks by frequency × interview weight, and redrill the top one within 48 hours. The interview line: ‘the mock is the test; the debrief is the studying.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

cards.front: How do you split attention in a combined design-plus-coding round?
cards.back: Design the path first (ten minutes, thinnest slice), then code only that slice end-to-end — a working vertical beats a broad stub. The interview line: ‘thin and working beats wide and broken.’

cards.front: What is the fullstack mock’s unique failure mode?
cards.back: Getting stuck in one layer: forty minutes on CSS while the API is unstarted. Timebox per layer and announce the switches. The interview line: ‘the layers are budgeted separately.’

cards.front: How do you prepare differently for startup vs big-company fullstack loops?
cards.back: Startups probe breadth and shipping speed (build the thing); big companies probe depth per layer (defend each choice). The interview line: ‘read the loop’s shape, then train for it.’

cards.front: The taper period’s rule is:
cards.back: **No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest** — Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

cards.front: Weak-spot triage should prioritize leaks by:
cards.back: **Frequency × interview weight — what costs the most points most often** — Expected value: fix what loses you the most points most often.

cards.front: A behavioral ledger prevents:
cards.back: **Repeating the same story across rounds and losing track of feedback** — Loops have multiple behavioral touchpoints; the ledger keeps each one fresh and improving.

cards.front: In an API-design round, idempotency belongs in the discussion because:

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Run a timed full-path design mock (45 min): 10 min path design, then the thinnest vertical slice — narrate tradeoffs, timebox visibly.
2. Run an API + auth deep-dive mock: defend the contract and the threat model against follow-ups — mechanism over buzzwords.
3. Run a live-coding-across-the-stack mock: one feature from UI to DB in the timebox — thin slice, working, narrated.
4. Run one behavioral round from the ledger: two-minute STAR answers, no repeated stories.
5. Debrief all four within the hour each: template, ranked leaks, 48-hour redrills, ledger update — then the taper plan.

cards.front: How do you show Optional mastery in a Swift interview?
cards.back: Binding (if let/guard let) over force-unwrapping, optional chaining for deep access, nil-coalescing for defaults, and ‘!!’ as a code smell you justify only with a proof. Map/flatMap on Optionals for transforms without pyramids.

cards.front: Value vs reference semantics — the Swift interview core?
cards.back: Structs/enums: copied on assignment (value semantics — no shared-state bugs). Classes: shared reference (identity matters: view controllers, shared services). Choose struct by default; reach for class when identity or inheritance is required.

cards.front: Why does Swift lean on protocols so hard?
cards.back: Protocol-oriented design: capabilities as protocols, shared behavior via protocol extensions with default implementations, generics constrained by protocols. The interview line: ‘prefer composition of protocols over class inheritance.’

cards.front: What Swift generics and protocol features do interviewers probe?
cards.back: Generic functions and types with constraints (where clauses), associated types in protocols, and opaque return types (some Protocol). The pitch: ‘generics move the check from runtime crashes to compile-time errors.’ Know the tradeoff: specialization speed versus code-size growth.

cards.front: Escaping vs non-escaping closures in Swift — the interview version?
cards.back: Non-escaping (the default): the closure runs before the function returns — no retain-cycle risk, and self can be captured implicitly. Escaping (@escaping): the closure is stored or runs later (completion handlers) — self must be explicit (weak/unowned) to avoid cycles. The interview line: ‘escaping means the closure outlives the call; that is when memory discipline starts.’

cards.front: How do you explain value-type copy-on-write in a Swift interview?
cards.back: Structs copy on assignment but collections share storage until mutation — copy-on-write gives value semantics without the copy cost. The interview line: ‘copy-on-write is value semantics with a performance escape hatch.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in Swift error handling?
cards.back: throwing functions with do-catch, typed errors as enums, try? vs try! discipline (never force-try in production paths), and Result for async boundaries. The interview line: ‘errors are values — model them like the domain.’

cards.front: How do you discuss property wrappers in an interview?
cards.back: Compiler-synthesized storage plus access logic: @State, @Published, and custom wrappers for validated or persisted properties. The interview line: ‘property wrappers move cross-cutting property logic into one reusable place.’

cards.front: Using try! is acceptable only when:
cards.back: **You can prove the call cannot fail (e.g. a bundled resource that ships with the app)** — try! converts failure into a crash — justifiable only with a proof, never with hope.

cards.front: A closure lets a function:
cards.back: **Access its outer scope’s variables after that scope has returned** — The captured environment outlives the enclosing call — that’s what makes private state possible.

cards.front: Swift enums with associated values give you:
cards.back: **Type-safe variants carrying data — the discriminated-union pattern, exhaustively switchable** — Associated values make each case carry its payload with compile-time exhaustiveness — the Swift answer to the discriminated union.

cards.front: Protocol extensions with default implementations enable:
cards.back: **Shared behavior across conforming types without a base class** — Mixins via extensions: types gain behavior by conforming, no inheritance chain required.

steps: Set the timer for a real interview slot; no pauses, no notes beyond what the format allows.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Optionals** — The type-level answer to null: binding (if let/guard let) over force-unwrapping, chaining for deep access, nil-coalescing for defaults — '!!' as a justified-only smell.
- **Optional map/flatMap** — Transforms over optionals without pyramid nesting — the functional spelling of 'if-let then transform.'
- **Value semantics** — Structs/enums copied on assignment — no shared-state bugs; the Swift default, chosen deliberately.
- **Reference semantics** — Classes with shared identity — for view controllers, shared services, and anywhere identity or inheritance is required.
- **Protocols** — Capabilities as contracts — the unit of abstraction Swift leans on hardest.
- **Protocol extensions** — Default implementations shared across conforming types — mixins without a base class: 'composition of protocols over class inheritance.'
- **Generics and associated types** — Constrained generic code over protocol requirements — the machinery behind Swift's standard library and your own reusable components.
- **Closures and capture lists** — Captured variables with explicit ownership: capture lists ([weak self]) breaking retain cycles — the memory-management interview core.
- **Error handling** — throws and Result: typed, explicit failure — try! justified only with a proof the call cannot fail, never with hope.
- **Retain cycles** — Strong reference loops (delegate patterns, closures capturing self) — broken with weak/unowned; the leak interviewers always probe.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Rewrite five force-unwraps from a sample file using binding, chaining, and coalescing — state aloud for each why the unwrap was unjustified.
2. Model one feature twice: as a struct and as a class — write the test that shows the value/reference difference, then state the choosing rule.
3. Design a small protocol hierarchy with protocol extensions for shared behavior: two conforming types, one extension, zero base classes.
4. Write a generic function with an associated-type constraint (a simple container or pipeline) — state the constraint's job in one sentence.
5. Fix a retain cycle in a closure-heavy sample: add the capture list, explain the cycle that existed, and verify the deinit fires.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Swift core portfolio. A playground or package demonstrating: optional-heavy API handling without force-unwraps, a struct-vs-class decision with the test proving the semantics, a protocol-oriented mini-design, one generic abstraction, and a retain-cycle fix with the before/after. Each with a one-paragraph interview-style explanation. Deliverable: the package plus explanations — language depth you can walk through.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: language depth is the opening of the iOS loop, not the loop — frameworks, concurrency, and architecture decide the rest, and this course confers no certificate. Swift also evolves yearly; verify details against the current language guide before interviewing.

notes.title: Worked example: Using try! is acceptable only when:
notes.body:
**Problem.** Using try! is acceptable only when:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** You can prove the call cannot fail (e.g. a bundled resource that ships with the app)
- **Why:** try! converts failure into a crash — justifiable only with a proof, never with hope.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *try!* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In Swift Language Core, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in Swift Language Core gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

cards.front: What must you know about UIViewController lifecycle?
cards.back: loadView → viewDidLoad (one-time setup) → viewWill/DidAppear (per-appearance work, start/stop observations) → viewWill/DidDisappear → deinit. The interview traps: doing per-appearance work in viewDidLoad, and leaking via unreleased observers.

cards.front: How do you discuss Auto Layout?
cards.back: Constraints as linear equations the solver satisfies; intrinsic content size vs explicit constraints; ambiguity and conflicts (and how you read the logs); performance (flatten deep hierarchies). The interview line: ‘I think in constraints, not frames.’

cards.front: How do you explain SwiftUI’s state trio?
cards.back: @State: view-local value state. @Binding: a reference to someone else’s state (child writes up). @ObservedObject/@StateObject: external reference-type models (StateObject owns the lifetime). The interview line: ‘state flows down, events flow up, ownership is explicit.’

cards.front: How do you explain the SwiftUI layout algorithm?
cards.back: Three steps, parent-driven: the parent proposes a size, the child chooses its size, the parent places it. One pass, no constraint solver — which is why GeometryReader and alignment guides exist for the cases the simple flow can’t express.

cards.front: How do you bridge UIKit and SwiftUI?
cards.back: UIViewRepresentable/UIViewControllerRepresentable to embed UIKit in SwiftUI; UIHostingController to embed SwiftUI in UIKit. The interview line: ‘interop is a migration strategy — wrap the legacy, write new code in SwiftUI.’

cards.front: How do you discuss diffable data sources in an interview?
cards.back: Snapshots describe the UI state; the framework diffs and animates the changes — no manual index-path math, no crash-prone batch updates. The interview line: ‘snapshots make the list a function of state.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in SwiftUI navigation?
cards.back: NavigationStack with value-typed destinations and path state: deep linking and programmatic navigation become data, not segues. The interview line: ‘navigation as data is testable navigation.’

cards.front: How do you explain the responder chain’s interview relevance?
cards.back: Events travel up the chain (view → controller → window → app) until handled — the mechanism behind target-action fallthrough and shake-to-undo. The interview line: ‘unhandled events climb until someone claims them.’

cards.front: Choosing per screen (not per religion) is the senior answer because:
cards.back: **Each framework has real gaps — pragmatism ships, purity stalls** — Interop exists precisely so teams can mix; dogma ignores the gaps.

cards.front: UIViewRepresentable exists to:
cards.back: **Wrap a UIView so it can live inside a SwiftUI hierarchy** — The representable protocol bridges the imperative UIKit world into declarative SwiftUI.

cards.front: In SwiftUI layout, the parent:
cards.back: **Proposes a size; the child decides; the parent places it** — The negotiate-propose-place flow runs in a single pass — fast, but less flexible than Auto Layout.

cards.front: @Binding exists so that:
cards.back: **A child can read and write a parent’s state without owning it** — Bindings are two-way lenses: the parent owns, the child edits through the lens.

notes.body:

cards.front: GCD in an interview: what do you need cold?
cards.back: Serial vs concurrent queues, QoS classes (user-interactive down to background), async vs sync dispatch, dispatch groups for fan-in, and the iron rule: UI on main, work off main. Deadlock demo: sync onto the current serial queue.

cards.front: OperationQueue vs GCD?
cards.back: OperationQueue: higher-level — dependencies between operations, cancellation, priorities, max concurrency. GCD: lighter, C-level queues. The interview line: ‘dependencies and cancellation buy the Operation abstraction; otherwise GCD.’

cards.front: How do you explain Swift’s structured concurrency?
cards.back: async/await for sequential-looking async code, tasks in hierarchies where children can’t outlive parents, actors for isolated mutable state. The interview line: ‘structure makes lifetimes provable — no more detached callbacks leaking.’

cards.front: What do actors buy you?
cards.back: Isolated mutable state with compiler-enforced exclusive access: only one task touches the actor’s state at a time, and the compiler flags data races at build time. The interview line: ‘actors make the compiler my concurrency reviewer.’

cards.front: Why is main-thread discipline non-negotiable on iOS?
cards.back: UIKit/SwiftUI are not thread-safe: UI updates off the main thread cause undefined behavior — glitches, crashes, corruption. The rule: compute off main (@MainActor for UI-bound code), hop back to main for every UI touch.

cards.front: How do you explain @MainActor in an interview?
cards.back: A global actor isolating UI-touching code to the main thread at compile time — the compiler, not discipline, enforces main-thread updates. The interview line: ‘@MainActor turns a convention into a guarantee.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in async sequences?
cards.back: AsyncSequence for streams of values over time (notifications, location updates) with for-await consumption and cancellation on task end. The interview line: ‘async sequences are async/await for streams.’

cards.front: How do you discuss thread-safety beyond ‘use the main thread’?
cards.back: Serial queues or actors for shared mutable state, immutable value types passed across threads, and locks only as a last resort with the shortest critical section. The interview line: ‘isolation beats locking — structure beats both.’

cards.front: @MainActor on a class guarantees:
cards.back: **Its methods run on the main thread — safe for UI work** — The compiler enforces the hop: UI-touching code can’t accidentally run elsewhere.

cards.front: Swift actors prevent data races by:
cards.back: **Enforcing exclusive, serialized access to their isolated state** — Isolation is checked at compile time: shared mutable state without synchronization can’t compile.

cards.front: Structured concurrency’s core guarantee is:
cards.back: **Child tasks can’t outlive their parent scope** — The task tree bounds lifetimes: cancellation and completion propagate through the structure.

cards.front: Operation dependencies give you:
cards.back: **Declarative ordering (‘B after A’) without manual synchronization** — The queue topologically sorts the graph; you declare relationships, not locks.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **GCD queues** — Serial vs concurrent queues; async vs sync dispatch — the iron rule: UI on main, work off main; the deadlock demo: sync onto the current serial queue.
- **QoS classes** — User-interactive down to background — priority as a scheduling hint the system actually honors.
- **Dispatch groups** — Fan-in: enter/leave across parallel work, notify on completion — the pre-async/await coordination primitive.
- **OperationQueue** — Higher-level: dependencies between operations, cancellation, priorities, max concurrency — 'dependencies and cancellation buy the abstraction; otherwise GCD.'
- **Structured concurrency** — async/await with task hierarchies where children can't outlive parents — lifetimes provable, no detached callbacks leaking.
- **@MainActor** — Compiler-enforced main-thread execution for UI-bound code — UI-touching code can't accidentally run elsewhere.
- **Actors** — Isolated mutable state with serialized, compiler-checked access — data races caught at build time: 'actors make the compiler my concurrency reviewer.'
- **Main-thread discipline** — UIKit/SwiftUI are not thread-safe: compute off main, hop back for every UI touch — undefined behavior otherwise.
- **Cooperative cancellation** — Tasks check for cancellation at suspension points — structured concurrency makes the propagation automatic.
- **Data-race safety** — The compile-time guarantee: shared mutable state without synchronization can't compile under strict concurrency.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write the GCD deadlock demo (sync onto the current serial queue), run it, then fix it — explain the mechanism aloud in under a minute.
2. Convert a dispatch-group fan-in to structured concurrency: task group with the same coordination, then state what the structure guarantees that the group didn't.
3. Isolate shared mutable state in an actor: show the data race the compiler now rejects, and the serialized access it enforces.
4. Audit a sample for main-thread violations: mark every UI touch, route them through @MainActor, and state the rule each fix enforces.
5. Build one screen's data load with async/await end to end: fetch off main, hop to main for UI, cancellation on disappear — the disciplined shape, complete.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Concurrency portfolio. A small app feature demonstrating: GCD done right (queues, QoS, groups), the structured-concurrency rewrite, an actor guarding shared state, and @MainActor-enforced UI updates — each with a before/after showing the hazard removed. Document the interview-style explanation per piece. Deliverable: the feature plus explanations — concurrency you can prove.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: Swift concurrency is still evolving — strict checking modes and best practices shift yearly, and this course confers no certificate. State which language mode your answers assume; interviewers respect the precision.

notes.title: Worked example: @MainActor on a class guarantees:
notes.body:
**Problem.** @MainActor on a class guarantees:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Its methods run on the main thread — safe for UI work
- **Why:** The compiler enforces the hop: UI-touching code can’t accidentally run elsewhere.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *The compiler enforces the hop: UI-touching code can’t accidentally run elsewhere.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In Concurrency on iOS, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in Concurrency on iOS gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

cards.front: What belongs in UserDefaults — and what doesn’t?
cards.back: Small user preferences (toggles, last-selected tab). NOT secrets (that’s Keychain), NOT large data, NOT anything needing queries or migrations. The interview line: ‘UserDefaults is a preferences plist, not a database.’

cards.front: How do you discuss Codable and file storage?
cards.back: Codable: compiler-synthesized serialization for JSON/plist — custom keys and strategies for real-world APIs. File storage: app sandbox directories (documents vs caches vs tmp) with the right protection. The interview line: ‘Codable for the format, the sandbox for the place.’

cards.front: Core Data stack in 60 seconds?
cards.back: Persistent container → managed object contexts (main for UI, background for work) → persistent store coordinator → SQLite. Faults are lazy loading; the interview traps are threading (one context per queue) and merge policies on conflicts.

cards.front: SwiftData at a glance — how do you position it?
cards.back: Apple’s modern persistence: @Model macro-driven, Swift-native queries with #Predicate, SwiftUI-integrated via @Query — backed by Core Data’s storage. The interview line: ‘SwiftData is the modern API; Core Data knowledge still explains what’s underneath.’

cards.front: Where do secrets go on iOS?
cards.back: Keychain — encrypted, access-controlled (kSecAttrAccessible), surviving app reinstall on the device. The interview line: ‘if it’s a secret, it’s in the Keychain; UserDefaults is a plist anyone can read.’

cards.front: How do you discuss CloudKit sync in an interview?
cards.back: Apple’s backend-as-a-service for iCloud sync: private/public/shared databases, subscriptions for push, and conflict resolution you must design for. The interview line: ‘CloudKit gives you sync; the merge policy is still yours.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in background data tasks?
cards.back: BGProcessingTask for deferrable work (sync, ML) with system-scheduled windows, and the discipline of short, resumable units. The interview line: ‘background work is a guest of the OS — behave like one.’

cards.front: How do you talk about data migration in Core Data?
cards.back: Lightweight migration for additive changes (automatic with a mapping model), heavyweight for the rest — and versioned models from day one. The interview line: ‘ship the versioned model before you need the migration.’

cards.front: The choosing rule’s core is:
cards.back: **Access pattern first — queries, relationships, and size decide the store** — Storage choice follows how data is read, written, and related — not habit.

cards.front: Keychain items vs UserDefaults for a refresh token:
cards.back: **Keychain: encrypted storage with access control; UserDefaults is plaintext-adjacent** — Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials — they get the strongest storage available.

cards.front: SwiftData’s @Query in SwiftUI provides:
cards.back: **Live-updating fetch results bound to the view — the UI refreshes as data changes** — Declarative data: the view describes what it needs and stays in sync automatically.

cards.front: Core Data faults are:
cards.back: **Lazily-loaded placeholders — data materializes on first access** — Faulting defers loading until the property is touched — memory-efficient by design.

cards.front: MVC vs MVVM on iOS — the honest comparison?
cards.back: MVC in UIKit decays into Massive View Controller; MVVM extracts state and logic into testable view models with the view as a binding layer. Coordinators own navigation so view controllers stop knowing about each other.

cards.front: How do you do dependency injection on iOS without a framework?
cards.back: Constructor injection as the default: pass dependencies through the initializer so they are explicit and testable. Use protocols for the seams, and an environment object or a composition root for app-wide assembly. The interview line: ‘DI on iOS is a design habit — protocols and initializers — before it is ever a framework.’

cards.front: What is unidirectional data flow?
cards.back: State flows down, events flow up: a single source of truth, views render from it, user actions dispatch events that produce new state. Debugging becomes ‘what event produced this state?’ The interview line: ‘one direction, one truth, no mysteries.’

cards.front: How do you layer mobile tests?
cards.back: Unit: view models/logic with fakes — fast, many. UI (XCUITest/Espresso): critical journeys — slow, few. Snapshot: visual regressions on components. The interview line: ‘I test logic in units and reserve devices for what only devices prove.’

cards.front: How do you discuss architecture tradeoffs in an interview?
cards.back: Name the forces (testability, team size, app complexity, longevity), the options with their costs, and your choice with the condition that would change it. The interview line: ‘every architecture is a bet — I state the odds.’

cards.front: How do you explain the coordinator pattern’s interview value?
cards.back: Coordinators own navigation flow so view controllers stop knowing about each other — deep linking and A/B flows become testable objects. The interview line: ‘navigation is a flow, not a view controller’s side effect.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in SwiftUI app architecture?
cards.back: State at the right level (@State local, @StateObject owned, @EnvironmentObject shared), the view as a pure function of state, and side effects isolated in observable models. The interview line: ‘SwiftUI architecture is state placement.’

cards.front: How do you discuss feature-flagged architecture on iOS?
cards.back: Flags evaluated at launch or fetched remotely, with the app degrading cleanly when flags are missing — kill switches for risky launches. The interview line: ‘flags decouple the App Store review clock from your release clock.’

cards.front: Stating what would change your architecture choice is strong because:

cards.front: Snapshot tests catch:
cards.back: **Unintended visual changes — pixel-level regressions in components** — Rendered-output comparison: the safety net for UI refactors.

cards.front: Unidirectional flow’s debugging win is:
cards.back: **State changes have a single traceable path — events in, state out** — Two-way bindings create update cycles; one direction makes every change explainable.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Massive View Controller** — UIKit MVC's decay mode: the view controller absorbs networking, logic, and navigation — the problem MVVM and coordinators solve.
- **MVVM** — State and logic extracted into testable view models; the view as a binding layer — testability as the payoff.
- **Coordinators** — Navigation owned outside view controllers — screens stop knowing about each other; flows become testable objects.
- **Dependency injection** — Classes declare needs, something else supplies them — constructor injection, testable with fakes, no manual singletons.
- **Unidirectional data flow** — State down, events up: one source of truth, one traceable path — 'one direction, one truth, no mysteries.'
- **Test pyramid (mobile)** — Unit: view models and logic with fakes — fast, many. UI (XCUITest): critical journeys — slow, few. Snapshot: visual regressions on components.
- **Seams** — The interfaces between layers — where testability and changeability live; 'I design the seams first — the code follows the seams.'
- **Conditional choices** — 'I chose X because [conditions]; I'd switch to Y if [change]' — the sentence that proves judgment over dogma.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Refactor one Massive View Controller into MVVM + coordinator: extract the view model, move navigation to the coordinator — state what each move bought.
2. Add DI to the refactored feature: constructor injection with fakes in tests — show the test that was impossible before.
3. Trace one user action through unidirectional flow: event up, state down — then break it deliberately (two-way binding) and observe the debugging cost.
4. Write the three test layers for one feature: unit tests on the view model, one UI test on the critical journey, one snapshot — state what each layer proves.
5. Argue one architecture choice aloud in two minutes: forces, options with costs, choice, and the condition that would change it — the bet with stated odds.

For a two-screen feature: the pattern choice (MVVM + coordinators + repository, or your argued alternative) with the forces analysis, the DI map, the unidirectional flow diagram, and the test plan across the three layers. Include the conditional: what would change your choice. Deliverable: the brief — architecture argued, not asserted.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: architecture taste is team- and app-shaped — the 'right' pattern depends on size, longevity, and who's maintaining it, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers reward the tradeoff argument; the codebase you inherit will have opinions of its own.

notes.title: Worked example: Stating what would change your architecture choice is strong because:
notes.body:
**Problem.** Stating what would change your architecture choice is strong because:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** It proves the choice was reasoned from conditions, not dogma
- **Why:** Conditional choices show engineering judgment; unconditional ones show fashion.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Conditional choices show engineering judgment; unconditional ones show fashion.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In App Architecture Patterns, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in App Architecture Patterns gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

cards.front: How do you attack a ‘list-detail with cache’ app spec?
cards.back: Layers: networking (async, cancellable) → repository (network + local cache, single source of truth) → view models (state) → UI. The interview line: ‘the repository is the only class that knows where data lives.’

cards.front: What does a good networking layer look like?
cards.back: Typed endpoints (Retrofit/URLSession), coroutine/async suspension, centralized error mapping, auth injection via interceptors, and cancellable requests tied to lifecycle. The interview line: ‘the UI never sees HTTP — it sees domain results.’

cards.front: How do you structure the data layer in the guided build?
cards.back: Repository pattern: the view model talks to a repository protocol, never to networking or storage directly. The repository merges network and local cache behind a single source of truth and exposes async streams. The interview line: ‘the repository is the seam that makes the build testable without the network.’

cards.front: How do you turn a guided build into an interview narrative?
cards.back: Problem → constraints → key decisions (with rejected alternatives) → result → what you’d do with more time. The build is proof; the narrative is the delivery vehicle — interviewers probe decisions, so lead with them.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'App spec: a list-detail app with cache'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: How do you handle image loading and caching in the build?
cards.back: Async loading with cancellation on reuse, an in-memory LRU plus disk cache, and downsampling to the display size — never the full image in a list cell. The interview line: ‘images are the fastest way to blow the memory budget.’

cards.front: How do you structure error states in the guided build?
cards.back: Typed errors mapped to user-facing states (offline, empty, failed) with retry actions — the UI never shows a raw error object. The interview line: ‘every failure is a designed screen.’

cards.front: What does the build’s test target look like?
cards.back: View-model unit tests with fake repositories, plus one UI test for the critical journey — fast, deterministic, no network. The interview line: ‘test the decisions, not the framework.’

cards.front: A build narrative should lead with:
cards.back: **The problem, constraints, and key decisions with alternatives** — Decisions are what get probed; leading with them controls the conversation.

cards.front: SwiftData’s @Query in SwiftUI provides:
cards.back: **Live-updating fetch results bound to the view — the UI refreshes as data changes** — Declarative data: the view describes what it needs and stays in sync automatically.

cards.front: Centralizing auth in an interceptor beats per-call headers because:
cards.back: **Token refresh and injection happen once — every call inherits it correctly** — Cross-cutting concerns in one place: no call site can forget the token.

cards.front: The repository’s job in the list-detail spec is:
cards.back: **Mediating network and cache — one data API for the view models** — View models stay source-agnostic; caching policy lives in one seam.

notes.title: Worked example: The taper period’s rule is:
notes.body:
**Problem.** The taper period’s rule is:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
- **Why:** Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Interviews test performance under pressure, not just knowledge. In iOS Mock Circuit, these habits lose offers:
- **Silent coding.** The interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear. Narrate: restate, propose, tradeoff, then code.
- **No complexity statement.** Finishing code without stating time and space complexity leaves the easiest points on the table. State it unprompted, every time.
- **Edge cases last.** Bolting on edge cases after 'done' signals shallow testing. Name them up front, handle them in the code, verify at the end.
- **Memorized solutions.** Reciting a known solution collapses the moment the interviewer twists the problem. Learn patterns and derivations, not scripts.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** 'No questions' reads as disinterest. Prepare questions that reveal how the team actually works.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every mock in iOS Mock Circuit gets a written review within a day: what broke, what held, one drill to fix the weakest rep.

cards.front: How do you demonstrate Kotlin null-safety depth?
cards.back: Nullable types (?), safe calls (?.), Elvis (?:) for defaults, !! as a justified-only escape hatch, and let/run scoping for non-null blocks. The platform-types warning: Java interop can still hand you null — annotate and defend at boundaries.

cards.front: Data classes vs sealed classes — when each?
cards.back: Data class: value holders with generated equals/hashCode/copy — UI state, DTOs. Sealed class/interface: closed hierarchies for states and results (Loading/Success/Error) with exhaustive when. Together they model UI state safely.

cards.front: What’s the coroutines mental model you’d state?
cards.back: Lightweight sequential-looking async: suspend functions pause without blocking threads, structured concurrency ties child lifetimes to scopes, dispatchers choose the thread pool (Main/IO/Default). ‘Sequential code, asynchronous execution.’

cards.front: Extension functions and scope functions — the interview version?
cards.back: Extensions add behavior without inheritance (nullable receivers included). Scope functions: let (transform nullable), apply (configure), run/with (compute on receiver), also (side effects). The interview line: ‘I pick the scope function by what it returns and what ‘it’ is.’

cards.front: What does Kotlin delegation give you?
cards.back: by lazy: thread-safe lazy init — expensive objects created once on first use. observable/vetoable: react to property changes. Class delegation (by): composition without boilerplate. The interview line: ‘delegation removes the ceremony around common patterns.’

cards.front: How do you explain reified type parameters?
cards.back: inline + reified keeps the type at runtime, defeating erasure for that call — enabling things like type-safe JSON parsing without a Class token. The interview line: ‘reified is erasure with an escape hatch.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in Kotlin flows beyond the basics?
cards.back: Cold vs hot (flow vs StateFlow/SharedFlow), operators as transformations, and exception transparency — plus testing with Turbine. The interview line: ‘flows are coroutines for streams of values.’

cards.front: How do you discuss Kotlin multiplatform in an interview?
cards.back: Shared business logic in common code with expect/actual for platform APIs — UI stays native. The interview line: ‘share the logic, not the pixels.’

cards.front: An inline function with a reified type parameter lets you:
cards.back: **Use the type at runtime — defeating erasure for that call (e.g. type-safe parsing without a Class token)** — inline + reified preserves the type argument at the call site — the standard workaround for JVM type erasure.

cards.front: by lazy is preferred over lateinit var when:
cards.back: **The value is immutable and expensive — initialized once, safely, on first access** — lazy gives val semantics with deferred cost; lateinit is a var promise the compiler can’t verify.

cards.front: let is the right scope function when you want to:
cards.back: **Transform a (possibly null) value and return the result** — let’s lambda returns its last expression — the transform-and-return shape.

cards.front: A suspend function differs from a blocking call in that it:
cards.back: **Suspends without blocking the underlying thread** — Suspension frees the thread for other coroutines; blocking would pin it.

Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

cards.front: Activities, fragments, lifecycles — what must you know cold?
cards.back: The lifecycle callbacks and what belongs in each (init in onCreate, cleanup symmetric in onDestroy), configuration changes destroying and recreating, and why ViewModels survive them. The interview line: ‘the lifecycle is a contract — I code against the callbacks, not around them.’

cards.front: How do you explain intents and the back stack?
cards.back: Intents: the messaging primitive — explicit (targeted) vs implicit (resolved by the system). The task back stack orders activities for back navigation; launch modes and intent flags shape it. Deep links are intents from the outside world.

cards.front: What must you know about Android view measurement?
cards.back: Measure pass (parent proposes, child measures via MeasureSpec: EXACTLY/AT_MOST/UNSPECIFIED) → layout pass (parent positions). Custom views implement onMeasure/onLayout. The interview line: ‘measure negotiates size; layout assigns position.’

cards.front: Services, broadcast receivers, WorkManager — when each?
cards.back: Foreground service: user-visible long work (playback). WorkManager: deferrable guaranteed work (sync, uploads) — the modern default. Broadcast receivers: system events. The interview line: ‘background work goes through WorkManager unless the user is actively engaged.’

cards.front: How do you discuss Android’s permissions model?
cards.back: Install-time vs runtime permissions, permission groups, one-time and while-in-use grants, and the UX rule: ask in context with a rationale, handle denial gracefully. The interview line: ‘permissions are a trust negotiation, not a manifest entry.’

cards.front: How do you explain the activity lifecycle’s interview edge cases?
cards.back: onPause is not for heavy work (the next activity waits), config changes recreate by default (ViewModel survives, the activity does not), and process death can kill you in the background — save state accordingly. The interview line: ‘the system can kill your process; design like it will.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in Jetpack Navigation?
cards.back: Single-activity with a nav graph: type-safe arguments, deep links as destinations, and back-stack manipulation as data. The interview line: ‘the graph makes navigation declarative and testable.’

cards.front: How do you discuss Doze and App Standby?
cards.back: The OS throttles background work to save battery: deferred jobs, batched network, restricted alarms — WorkManager is the compliant path. The interview line: ‘background work runs on the OS’s schedule, not yours.’

cards.front: Requesting a runtime permission should happen:
cards.back: **In context, when the feature needs it, with a clear rationale** — In-context requests with rationale get granted; upfront bulk requests get denied.

cards.front: WorkManager is preferred over a background service for deferrable work because:
cards.back: **It’s battery-aware, survives app restarts, and respects Doze — guaranteed execution** — The OS cooperates with WorkManager scheduling; raw background services get killed.

cards.front: MeasureSpec.AT_MOST means:
cards.back: **The child can be up to this size — wrap_content’s mode** — AT_MOST bounds the child; EXACTLY fixes it; UNSPECIFIED leaves it free.

cards.front: An explicit intent differs from an implicit intent in that it:
cards.back: **Names its target component directly; implicit intents are resolved by the system** — Explicit = ‘open this screen’; implicit = ‘who can handle this action?’ — resolved via intent filters.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Lifecycle as contract** — Init in onCreate, symmetric cleanup in onDestroy — code against the callbacks, not around them; ViewModels survive what activities don't.
- **Configuration changes** — Destroy-and-recreate on rotation — the reason state lives in ViewModels, not activities.
- **Intents** — The messaging primitive: explicit (targeted at a component) vs implicit (resolved by the system via intent filters) — deep links are intents from outside.
- **Task back stack** — The ordered activities behind the back button — shaped by launch modes and intent flags; the navigation model interviews assume.
- **Measure/layout passes** — Measure negotiates size (MeasureSpec: EXACTLY/AT_MOST/UNSPECIFIED), layout assigns position — custom views implement onMeasure/onLayout.
- **Foreground service** — User-visible long work (playback) — the only long-running background shape the user consents to.
- **WorkManager** — Deferrable guaranteed work (sync, uploads): battery-aware, survives restarts, respects Doze — the modern default for background work.
- **Broadcast receivers** — System-event hooks — for reacting to the outside world, not for doing the work itself.
- **Permissions model** — Install-time vs runtime, groups, one-time and while-in-use grants — 'permissions are a trust negotiation, not a manifest entry.'
- **In-context permission requests** — Ask when the feature needs it, with a rationale, handle denial gracefully — the UX rule that decides grant rates.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Trace an activity through rotation, back-press, and process death on paper: name every callback and what state survives each — then verify with logging.
2. Route three navigations (in-app, deep link, share intent): explicit vs implicit, the intent flags shaping the back stack — state the resolution rule each time.
3. Implement a custom view's onMeasure/onLayout for a simple layout: predict the MeasureSpec modes, verify with logging, fix the AT_MOST wrap_content case.
4. Schedule one deferrable job three ways (raw service, receiver, WorkManager): write the honest comparison — then keep the WorkManager version and state why.
5. Implement one runtime-permission flow in context with rationale and graceful denial — the trust-negotiation shape, complete.

cards.front: What’s the coroutines mental model you’d state?
cards.back: Lightweight sequential-looking async: suspend functions pause without blocking threads, structured concurrency ties child lifetimes to scopes, dispatchers choose the thread pool (Main/IO/Default). ‘Sequential code, asynchronous execution.’

cards.front: How do you explain Android’s structured concurrency?
cards.back: Coroutines run in scopes with lifetimes: viewModelScope for UI work, lifecycleScope for UI-bound tasks, and custom scopes with SupervisorJob for independent children. Children cannot outlive their scope — cancellation propagates downward. The interview line: ‘structured concurrency ties async work to a lifecycle, so nothing leaks past its owner.’

cards.front: StateFlow vs SharedFlow?
cards.back: StateFlow: hot, holds the latest value, replays to new collectors — UI state. SharedFlow: hot, configurable replay/buffer — one-shot events (with the caveat that events are better modeled as state where possible). Both respect structured concurrency.

cards.front: Why viewModelScope?
cards.back: It’s a CoroutineScope tied to the ViewModel’s lifecycle — cancelled automatically on ViewModel clearance. No leaked coroutines on rotation, no manual cleanup. The interview point: structured concurrency makes lifecycle bugs impossible by construction.

cards.front: How do cancellation and exceptions interact in coroutines?
cards.back: Cancellation is cooperative (checkpoints at suspension points); a child’s failure cancels the scope by default — supervisorScope isolates sibling failures. CoroutineExceptionHandler catches uncaught exceptions in root coroutines. The interview line: ‘failure policy is a design choice, stated up front.’

cards.front: How do you explain dispatchers in an interview?
cards.back: Dispatchers.Main for UI, Dispatchers.IO for blocking I/O (file, network), Dispatchers.Default for CPU work — withContext switches without callback nesting. The interview line: ‘dispatchers are thread pools with intent.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in flow exception handling?
cards.back: catch upstream of collection, SupervisorJob semantics for independent children, and coroutineExceptionHandler only for uncaught crashes. The interview line: ‘handle where you can recover; let the scope handle the rest.’

cards.front: How do you test coroutines in an interview answer?
cards.back: runTest with a test dispatcher: virtual time, deterministic delays, Turbine for flow assertions — no sleeps, no flakes. The interview line: ‘virtual time makes async tests synchronous.’

cards.front: RxJava Disposables correspond to coroutine:
cards.back: **Jobs/scopes — the thing you cancel to stop the work** — Both represent cancellable async work; disposing is Rx’s structured-concurrency equivalent.

cards.front: supervisorScope differs from coroutineScope in that:
cards.back: **A child’s failure doesn’t cancel its siblings** — Supervision isolates failures: one failing child doesn’t take down independent siblings.

cards.front: viewModelScope’s cancellation guarantee means:
cards.back: **Launched coroutines are cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared — no leaks on rotation** — Scope cancellation propagates to children: rotation can’t strand work anymore.

cards.front: StateFlow suits UI state because:
cards.back: **It always holds the latest value and replays it to new collectors** — New collectors (e.g. after rotation) immediately get current state — no missed updates.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Suspend functions** — Sequential-looking async that pauses without blocking threads — the unit of coroutine work.
- **Dispatchers** — Main (UI), IO (blocking I/O), Default (CPU work) — the pool choice made explicit per call.
- **Structured concurrency** — Child lifetimes tied to scopes: cancellation and completion propagate through the structure — no detached work leaking.
- **coroutineScope vs supervisorScope** — coroutineScope: a child's failure cancels siblings. supervisorScope: failures isolated — 'failure policy is a design choice, stated up front.'
- **Cold flows** — Start work per collector — the stream that doesn't exist until observed.
- **StateFlow** — Hot, holds the latest value, replays to new collectors — UI state; rotation-safe by construction.
- **SharedFlow** — Hot, configurable replay/buffer — one-shot events (with the caveat that events are often better modeled as state).
- **viewModelScope** — A CoroutineScope tied to the ViewModel lifecycle — cancelled automatically on clearance; no leaked coroutines on rotation.
- **Cooperative cancellation** — Checkpoints at suspension points — cancellation propagates through structured scopes automatically.
- **RxJava literacy** — Disposables as the Jobs/scopes equivalent — the legacy vocabulary for the codebases you'll inherit.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Convert a callback chain to suspend functions with explicit dispatchers: state the thread each part runs on before and after.
2. Build a task hierarchy with coroutineScope, fail one child, observe the sibling cancellation — then switch to supervisorScope and observe the isolation.
3. Model one screen's state in StateFlow and its one-shot events in SharedFlow: rotate the device and verify the state replay; state the events-as-state caveat.
4. Launch work in viewModelScope, rotate, and verify cancellation — then write the sentence: 'structured concurrency makes this leak impossible by construction.'
5. Translate one RxJava chain (map/filter/dispose) to coroutines/Flow: name the Disposable→Job mapping at each step — the literacy drill for legacy code.

Deliverable: the feature plus explanations — modern concurrency, proven.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: coroutines are the current idiom, not the eternal one — RxJava still runs production code you'll inherit, and this course confers no certificate. Literacy in both is the honest position; fluency in the modern one is the interview position.

notes.title: Worked example: RxJava Disposables correspond to coroutine:
